Plus Codes are like street addresses for people or places that don’t have one. Instead of addresses with street names and numbers, Plus Codes are based on latitude and longitude, and displayed as numbers and letters.

## Why Plus Codes?

![Image 32](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/9dc3448960e80f72dbccdeed77dcddc8c6fa4da5.svg)

Open source and easy to use

Plus Codes technology is open source and free to create and use. They are much shorter than traditional global coordinates, so they're easy to share.

![Image 33](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/617f07c2232fbfffea814375caf6ff98d9a2b5c9.svg)

Accessible offline

Plus Codes work whether you're online or offline—you don't need an internet connection.

![Image 34](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/0dd4c50ecce352ab4a741db8a640d760806c96ae.svg)

Language independent

Plus Codes are based on a set of 20 alphanumeric characters. They exclude vowels and confusing characters, and are not case-sensitive.

![Image 35](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/651b5eddda4d5b55b913b535752de3cbd9c70488.svg)

Versatile

Plus Codes represent an area. The resolution of the area can be changed by adding or removing characters after the "+" sign.

## Why Plus Codes?

![Image 32](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/9dc3448960e80f72dbccdeed77dcddc8c6fa4da5.svg)

Open source and easy to use

Plus Codes technology is open source and free to create and use. They are much shorter than traditional global coordinates, so they're easy to share.

![Image 33](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/617f07c2232fbfffea814375caf6ff98d9a2b5c9.svg)

Accessible offline

Plus Codes work whether you're online or offline—you don't need an internet connection.

![Image 34](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/0dd4c50ecce352ab4a741db8a640d760806c96ae.svg)

Language independent

Plus Codes are based on a set of 20 alphanumeric characters. They exclude vowels and confusing characters, and are not case-sensitive.

![Image 35](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/651b5eddda4d5b55b913b535752de3cbd9c70488.svg)

Versatile

Plus Codes represent an area. The resolution of the area can be changed by adding or removing characters after the "+" sign.

The code is combined with a nearby town or locality, such as "MQQH+W7 Woodley, Nairobi, Kenya". (If there is no town or locality nearby, longer codes exist that are globally unique "6GCRMQQH+W7".)

You can give plus codes to other people, and tell them to find you using this website or Google Maps.

With a plus code, someone can find their way straight to you - getting there easier and faster. Plus codes are completely free to have and use.

For many of us, it’s easy to take addresses for granted. We order products online, and they show up at our doorstep. In an emergency, we give our address to an ambulance or fire truck, and they quickly get to us. But what happens when you don’t have an address and you need to direct someone to your current location?

More than 2 billion people on the planet—about 25 percent of us or more —either don’t have an address or have an address that isn’t easy to locate. To tackle this challenge, we launched [Plus Codes](https://plus.codes/) in 2015. Plus Codes are simple, easy to use digital addresses derived from latitude and longitude coordinates. They can be used to uniquely identify any location, from a rural home out on a prairie to a small shop stall on a nameless street.

Today we’ve made it easier for anyone with an Android device to share their location using Plus Codes in Google Maps. People who use Google Maps might be familiar with the blue dot that represents their current location. Simply tap the blue dot to get a Plus Code for your current location that can be shared with others as easily as giving them a phone number.

![Image 2: Tap the blue dot to get a Plus Code](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/original_images/Plus_Codes_blue_dot.gif)

### Plus Codes: free, digital address for anywhere

A Plus Code is a simple alphanumeric code which can be combined with a locality (for example: FWM8+V9, Ibadan, Nigeria). They look like a regular address, but with a short code where a street name or number would be. Beyond using the blue dot, you can also find the Plus Code for a location by tapping and holding the map to drop a pin at a location you want a Plus Code for.

Plus Codes are searchable on Google Maps and even Google Search, meaning everywhere on the planet can now be uniquely identified.

These digital location identifiers are free to use, available offline and can be printed on paper, posters and signs. The technology to generate Plus Codes is also [open source](https://opensource.google/projects/open-location-code), which means the technology is easy and free to use, so anyone can see how the technology works and develop their own applications for any use case.

![Image 3: About Plus Codes](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/original_images/About_Plus_Codes.gif)

### A helpful tool for emergency and crisis situations

Plus Codes can be especially helpful for people and organizations in emergency and crisis response scenarios. If you’ve ever been in an emergency, you know that being able to share your location for help to easily find you is critical. Yet in many places in the world, organizations struggle with this challenge on a daily basis.

With Plus Codes, not only can people share their location quickly even without an address, but they can now do so by simply opening up Google Maps and tapping on the blue dot to view, copy and share their Plus Code location. A Plus Code can then be entered into Google Maps to help locate and navigate to that location.

Digital locations through Plus Codes means that everywhere now has an easily identifiable location, saving time and getting resources there when it really matters. Not having an address should no longer be a barrier to easily sharing your location with service providers, guiding them to you when you most need them.

Download the latest version of the Google Maps Android app over the coming weeks to try out the new update.

For many of us, it’s easy to take addresses for granted. We order products online, and they show up at our doorstep. In an emergency, we give our address to an ambulance or fire truck, and they quickly get to us. But what happens when you don’t have an address and you need to direct someone to your current location?

More than 2 billion people on the planet—about 25 percent of us or more —either don’t have an address or have an address that isn’t easy to locate. To tackle this challenge, we launched [Plus Codes](https://plus.codes/) in 2015. Plus Codes are simple, easy to use digital addresses derived from latitude and longitude coordinates. They can be used to uniquely identify any location, from a rural home out on a prairie to a small shop stall on a nameless street.

Today we’ve made it easier for anyone with an Android device to share their location using Plus Codes in Google Maps. People who use Google Maps might be familiar with the blue dot that represents their current location. Simply tap the blue dot to get a Plus Code for your current location that can be shared with others as easily as giving them a phone number.

![Image 2: Tap the blue dot to get a Plus Code](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/original_images/Plus_Codes_blue_dot.gif)

### Plus Codes: free, digital address for anywhere

A Plus Code is a simple alphanumeric code which can be combined with a locality (for example: FWM8+V9, Ibadan, Nigeria). They look like a regular address, but with a short code where a street name or number would be. Beyond using the blue dot, you can also find the Plus Code for a location by tapping and holding the map to drop a pin at a location you want a Plus Code for.

Plus Codes are searchable on Google Maps and even Google Search, meaning everywhere on the planet can now be uniquely identified.

These digital location identifiers are free to use, available offline and can be printed on paper, posters and signs. The technology to generate Plus Codes is also [open source](https://opensource.google/projects/open-location-code), which means the technology is easy and free to use, so anyone can see how the technology works and develop their own applications for any use case.

![Image 3: About Plus Codes](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/original_images/About_Plus_Codes.gif)

### A helpful tool for emergency and crisis situations

Plus Codes can be especially helpful for people and organizations in emergency and crisis response scenarios. If you’ve ever been in an emergency, you know that being able to share your location for help to easily find you is critical. Yet in many places in the world, organizations struggle with this challenge on a daily basis.

With Plus Codes, not only can people share their location quickly even without an address, but they can now do so by simply opening up Google Maps and tapping on the blue dot to view, copy and share their Plus Code location. A Plus Code can then be entered into Google Maps to help locate and navigate to that location.

Digital locations through Plus Codes means that everywhere now has an easily identifiable location, saving time and getting resources there when it really matters. Not having an address should no longer be a barrier to easily sharing your location with service providers, guiding them to you when you most need them.

Download the latest version of the Google Maps Android app over the coming weeks to try out the new update.

**Eh?**

**So while browsing Google maps today, I noticed that along with the regular street, town, region and country information for a given place there was a small but intriguing combination of letters and numbers (and a plus, obviously).**

It was neatly tucked away in all the other details like it has always been there – but it hasn’t!

Here’s what I found:

1.   What are Plus Codes?
2.   How do I use Plus Codes?
3.   How are Plus Codes useful?

## What are Plus Codes?

A quick Google later and I am on Google Maps’ Plus Codes – explaining to me that they’re a way of encoding longitude and latitude data into a Plus Code and an area or area code (the area/area code is needed unless you’re within 25 kilometres of the location).

A Plus Code covers the area of a building (unless a high accuracy code is generated) up to 14×14 metre resolution. Adding one other character to the code provides resolution up to 3×3 metre. There’s not really that much to the codes, they’re just an area code and a local code.

I’d been looking for the exact location of Boris Brejcha’s [DJ set](https://youtu.be/4Rc-NGWEHdU) in the grounds of Château de Fontainebleau, France.

So, the reason I found them useful is because they can describe the location of the YouTube video (and my desk in the 20i office) much more precisely than the official addresses:

20i office 4VJ5+JG Mansfield, UK
YouTube video CM2X+RH Fontainebleau, France

## How do I use Plus Codes?

To get started with them, you don’t need to do much!

Choose your favourite language from those available – then find the longitude and latitude of a location and get encoding. Or get the Plus Code of a location and get decoding!

### Encoding a Plus Code

I decided to generate a code for the [castle](https://goo.gl/maps/VvCew5nu1Uz) using the coordinates from Google Maps. I used the raw source from Google’s [GitHub](https://github.com/google/open-location-code/tree/master/js/src), pasted it into my Chrome console, and used https://github.com/google/open-location-code/tree/master/js to find out what to do:

```
<= OpenLocationCode.encode(48.402096, 2.698874, OpenLocationCode.CODE_PRECISION_NORMAL)

=> "8FW4CM2X+RG"
```

Worked first time, so now it’s time to decode!

### Decoding a Plus code

Continuing their documentation I tried to decode my first encoded code:

```
<= OpenLocationCode.decode("8FW4CM2X+RG")

=> Object {
codeLength: 10
latitudeCenter: 48.402062500000014
latitudeHi: 48.40212500000001
latitudeLo: 48.402000000000015
longitudeCenter: 2.6988125000000167
longitudeHi: 2.6988750000000152
longitudeLo: 2.698750000000018
}
```

Also worked first time! There’s my original input data right there (give or take a few points difference).

## What are Plus Codes useful for?

They’re great for finding the location of a place that doesn’t have a perfect street address: the 20i office isn’t directly at the pin for our official postal address in Google Maps, but it is if you use the Plus Code.

[![Image 9: The location of 20i's door using a Plus Code](https://www.20i.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/20i-office-Plus-Code.png)](https://www.20i.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/20i-office-Plus-Code.png)
It is the same case for the location of Boris Brejcha’s DJ set inside the gardens at the castle: each place’s exact location given in a small handy code – awesome!

## Get on the map with Plus Codes

According to the World Bank, half of the world’s population live on ‘unnamed streets’. So for those people, Plus Codes are a way for them to have a recorded address – to receive deliveries and access services. They can even be used by emergency services or disaster relief in remote locations.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LJ9zEkXearU)

They were developed by Google, and they’re also known as Open Location Codes.

Well, that’s up to you I guess! Do you own a paintball centre whose location is difficult to describe? Do you own an oil company whose pumps’ locations are also difficult describe? You see what I’m getting at.

Find out more – [https://plus.codes/](https://plus.codes/)

![Image 15](https://community-cdn.openstreetmap.org/user_avatar/community.openstreetmap.org/reino_baptista/48/15327_2.png) Reino_Baptista:



> Is the use of plus codes be considered (to find places) in any OSM umbrella apps and sites?

How do you think they should be used?  
 Keeping in mind that +Codes does not indicate a point that can be defined with a coordinate but rather an area.  
 Would you be willing to add a +Code for each OSM element size?  
 I mean using the +Codes API to roughly define an area, i.e. a building would be equal to a +Codes with a certain number of digits, a town would be equivalent to a +Codes with fewer digits than the building.

[![Image 16: Screenshot_20250422-215309~2](https://community-cdn.openstreetmap.org/uploads/default/optimized/3X/0/3/034f846c5ebedb9a816ccb22e50098ea97b54178_2_274x500.png) Screenshot_20250422-215309~2 720×1313 80.8 KB](https://community-cdn.openstreetmap.org/uploads/default/original/3X/0/3/034f846c5ebedb9a816ccb22e50098ea97b54178.png "Screenshot_20250422-215309~2")

Or use a +Codes with a predetermined number of digits to identify any OSM element? Which, in my opinion, would be a bad idea to use +Codes, because this can be done with coordinates or with current OSM geocoding.  
 Should +Codes be added in full? I mean both encoding and decoding.  
 I suppose that in the future and to be more precise, we must define what we want to use: +Codes or OLC?; +Codes refers to a service directly related to Google Maps and that works without a Google ApiKey and with a Google ApiKey (The codes generated by OLC are called +Codes but it is also a web tool). Adding a Google ApiKey to the body of the query URL gives an extra in the returned information (Local Code).  
 Example of +Codes without Google ApiKey and with ApiKey Google.:

[![Image 17: Screenshot_20250422-222022~2](https://community-cdn.openstreetmap.org/uploads/default/original/3X/8/9/892e4f4c61fef344debd12e21553271e1fe5195c.png) Screenshot_20250422-222022~2 720×446 35 KB](https://community-cdn.openstreetmap.org/uploads/default/original/3X/8/9/892e4f4c61fef344debd12e21553271e1fe5195c.png "Screenshot_20250422-222022~2")

I think we should first define what use OLC would be given in OpenStreetMap:

*   Point to any area
*   Point to an OSM element.
*   Or the previous two.

Overview

Plus codes make location information easier to use. Instead of two long numbers (atitude and longitude) there's a single, shorter code.

Most people in the world live on an unnamed street. Plus codes were created so that these people can have an address, so that they can receive deliveries, access emergency services, register to vote – and more. Plus codes are open source and free to use, for any purpose, forever.

Plus codes are based on latitude and longitude, so they already exist everywhere. The location 47°21'56.0"N 8°31'29.3"E has the plus code "8FVC9G8F+6W".

Plus codes can be converted to plus code addresses. These use place names and a short version of the code: "9G8F+6W, Zürich, Switzerland". This form is easier to recognise, and the shorter code means people have less digits to remember.

This add-on for Google Sheets allows you to convert between location coordinates and plus codes, using a menu function and additional sheet functions:

*  PLUSCODE
*  PLUSCODE_CENTER
*  PLUSCODE_LENGTH
*  PLUSCODE_BOUNDS

You can also convert between plus codes and addresses using the menu and additional functions:

*  PLUSCODE_TO_ADDRESS
*  PLUSCODE_FROM_ADDRESS

Plus codes use the Open Location Code algorithm, an open source Google project. See https://opensource.google.com/projects/open-location-code for links to the open source projects.

Overview

Plus codes make location information easier to use. Instead of two long numbers (atitude and longitude) there's a single, shorter code.

Most people in the world live on an unnamed street. Plus codes were created so that these people can have an address, so that they can receive deliveries, access emergency services, register to vote – and more. Plus codes are open source and free to use, for any purpose, forever.

Plus codes are based on latitude and longitude, so they already exist everywhere. The location 47°21'56.0"N 8°31'29.3"E has the plus code "8FVC9G8F+6W".

Plus codes can be converted to plus code addresses. These use place names and a short version of the code: "9G8F+6W, Zürich, Switzerland". This form is easier to recognise, and the shorter code means people have less digits to remember.

This add-on for Google Sheets allows you to convert between location coordinates and plus codes, using a menu function and additional sheet functions:

*  PLUSCODE
*  PLUSCODE_CENTER
*  PLUSCODE_LENGTH
*  PLUSCODE_BOUNDS

You can also convert between plus codes and addresses using the menu and additional functions:

*  PLUSCODE_TO_ADDRESS
*  PLUSCODE_FROM_ADDRESS

Plus codes use the Open Location Code algorithm, an open source Google project. See https://opensource.google.com/projects/open-location-code for links to the open source projects.

# How to Find the Plus Code for Any Location

Posted on April 1, 2018 |  by [Prolific Oaktree](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/author/admin/)

If you want to find a Plus Code for a certain location, it is not that easy. At this point, you can’t do it on Google Maps. When you left-click on an area and choose What’s here?, it will give you latitude and longitude but Maps does not give you the Plus Code.

![Image 4: Google Maps What's Here](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/whats_here.png)

Place info on Google Maps

![Image 6: Latitude and Longitute](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/lat_long.png)

Latitude and longitude

However, what you can do is, you can go to [plus.codes](https://plus.codes/) and use the Find your code option.

![Image 8: Plus Codes Website](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/plus_codes_site.png)

plus.codes

Zoom in or out until the area that you want fills the screen. A Plus Code designates an area in the shape of a rectangle. It’s not a point like latitude and longitude. You can take advantage of that by zooming in and out until you get to the size of an area that you want. After you have the right area, go to the menu and choose the option to see the Grid.

![Image 10: Menu on plus codes site](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/menu.png)

Map menu

![Image 12: Grip option on menu](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/menu_grid.png)

Option to show grid

### Video explanation

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rj2wnzvU2r8)

After choosing the option to show the grid, you will see the rectangles that are available to you. In this case, the area labeled 86FVCF fits Hocking Hills State Park which is the area that I am looking for. 86FVCF is the first part of the full Plus Code that you will see later in this article.

![Image 14: Seeing 86FV in grid](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/86FV.png)

Grid shown over map

There is also a shortened code available at the bottom of the screen. CFG7+JP, works for anyone that lives close to the park. It’s a shortened, partial version of the code. CFG7+JP does not contain the beginning 86FV portion of the 86FVCF code, so it works when you are already relatively close to the area.

![Image 16: Plus code](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/plus_code.png)

Shortened Plus Code

On the left side of the plus.codes screen, you will see the full Plus Code and the shortened Plus Code that can be used for local navigation. # How to Find the Plus Code for Any Location

Posted on April 1, 2018 |  by [Prolific Oaktree](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/author/admin/)

If you want to find a Plus Code for a certain location, it is not that easy. At this point, you can’t do it on Google Maps. When you left-click on an area and choose What’s here?, it will give you latitude and longitude but Maps does not give you the Plus Code.

![Image 4: Google Maps What's Here](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/whats_here.png)

Place info on Google Maps

![Image 6: Latitude and Longitute](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/lat_long.png)

Latitude and longitude

However, what you can do is, you can go to [plus.codes](https://plus.codes/) and use the Find your code option.

![Image 8: Plus Codes Website](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/plus_codes_site.png)

plus.codes

Zoom in or out until the area that you want fills the screen. A Plus Code designates an area in the shape of a rectangle. It’s not a point like latitude and longitude. You can take advantage of that by zooming in and out until you get to the size of an area that you want. After you have the right area, go to the menu and choose the option to see the Grid.

![Image 10: Menu on plus codes site](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/menu.png)

Map menu

![Image 12: Grip option on menu](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/menu_grid.png)

Option to show grid

### Video explanation

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rj2wnzvU2r8)

After choosing the option to show the grid, you will see the rectangles that are available to you. In this case, the area labeled 86FVCF fits Hocking Hills State Park which is the area that I am looking for. 86FVCF is the first part of the full Plus Code that you will see later in this article.

![Image 14: Seeing 86FV in grid](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/86FV.png)

Grid shown over map

There is also a shortened code available at the bottom of the screen. CFG7+JP, works for anyone that lives close to the park. It’s a shortened, partial version of the code. CFG7+JP does not contain the beginning 86FV portion of the 86FVCF code, so it works when you are already relatively close to the area.

![Image 16: Plus code](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/plus_code.png)

Shortened Plus Code

On the left side of the plus.codes screen, you will see the full Plus Code and the shortened Plus Code that can be used for local navigation. If you want the entire Plus Code, which is probably the best practice if you are copy/pasting, go to the left of the screen and copy it. This is your full Plus Code. It’s not case-sensitive, but since we’re copy and pasting it in, it doesn’t matter.

![Image 18: Codes](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/codes.png)

Left side of plus.codes showing full and shortened Plus Codes

Go back to your mapping program, which is Google Maps in this case, and enter this Open Location Code into the search bar. Google Maps will go to the area that corresponds to the Plus Code and drop a pin in the middle of it. Maps shows you the latitude and longitude of the center of the Plus Code but it will not show the grid with the codes on it.

![Image 20: Plus code in Google Maps](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/plus_in_maps.jpg)

Google Maps searching for Plus Code

![Image 22: Hocking Hills on Map](https://www.prolificoaktree.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/hocking_hills.png)

After searching for Plus Code

Now you know how to find your Plus Code using plus.codes with the grid feature turned on and you can take that Plus Code and enter it into Google Maps, you know how to find and use a Plus Code. I hope that was helpful!

The country is separated from Indonesia by the Singapore Strait and from Malaysia by the Straits of Johor. It is interesting that the country is located just 1 degree north of the equator.

# Singapore

Latitude and longitude coordinates are: **1.290270, 103.851959**.

[Cities](https://www.latlong.net/tag?t=cities "Cities")[Botanic Paradise](https://www.latlong.net/tag?t=botanic-paradise "Botanic Paradise")[Multicultural City](https://www.latlong.net/tag?t=multicultural-city "Multicultural City")[Coastal City](https://www.latlong.net/tag?t=coastal-city "Coastal City")[Tourist Attractions](https://www.latlong.net/tag?t=tourist-attractions "Tourist Attractions")[City Of The Future](https://www.latlong.net/tag?t=city-of-the-future "City Of The Future")[Capital City](https://www.latlong.net/tag?t=capital-city "Capital City")

**Singapore**, officially known as the _Republic of Singapore_, is a famous city-state located on the **Malay** peninsula and is known as one of the world's leading commercial, business, cultural, and technological centers on the planet. The location of the country is interesting and its area includes 59 islands of various sizes. The country is separated from Indonesia by the Singapore Strait and from Malaysia by the Straits of Johor. It is interesting that the country is located just 1 degree north of the equator.

Singapore is a destination for tourists and for those who are looking for some great business opportunities in the Far East. It is known for its excellent modern infrastructure, a steadily boosting economy, numerous skyscrapers and shopping malls, and many other places of interest. Singapore is an independent country with an amazing and highly educated multicultural community, a global city, an economic miracle, and one of the most popular tourist cities in the world.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xi6r3hZe5Tg)

As the country is small, there are no large industrial or heavy producing facilities, and the country's economy is rather focused on finance, engineering, IT and design, and so on. Besides, Singapore is famous for its world-class services, and companies such as Singapore Airlines. Tourist attractions in Singapore include Universal Studios Singapore, Wings of Time, ArtScience Museum, National Gallery Singapore, Marina Barrage, **Singapore Botanic Gardens**, and so on. [**Singapore Changi Airport**](https://www.latlong.net/place/singapore-changi-airport-singapore-27493.html), with four modern terminals, serves the area.

[Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") is a [city-state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-state "City-state") and [island country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_country "Island country") in [maritime Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_Southeast_Asia "Maritime Southeast Asia"), located at the end of the [Malayan Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayan_Peninsula "Malayan Peninsula") between [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia") and [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia") as well as the [Straits of Malacca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Malacca "Straits of Malacca") and the [South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea"). It is highly compact and urbanised. As of 2026, Singapore has a total land area of approximately 744.3 square kilometres (287.4 sq mi).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-total_area_of_Singapore-1) Singapore is separated from Indonesia by the [Singapore Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_Strait "Singapore Strait") and from Malaysia by the [Straits of Johor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Johor "Straits of Johor").

Geographically, Singapore comprises its [mainland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_Island "Singapore Island") and other islands. The mainland of Singapore measures 50 kilometres (31 mi) from east to west and 27 kilometres (17 mi) from north to south with 193 kilometres (120 mi) of coastline. These figures are based on 2.515 metres (8 ft 3.0 in) High Water Mark [cadastral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadastre "Cadastre") survey boundaries.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-Department_of_Statistics_Singapore-2) It has an [exclusive economic zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclusive_economic_zone "Exclusive economic zone") of 1,067 km 2 (412 mi 2).

## Topography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Topography")]

See also: [List of islands of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Singapore "List of islands of Singapore") and [Extreme points of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_points_of_Singapore "Extreme points of Singapore")

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Upper_Seletar_Reservoir_5%2C_Oct_05.JPG/250px-Upper_Seletar_Reservoir_5%2C_Oct_05.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Seletar_Reservoir_5,_Oct_05.JPG)

Upper Seletar Reservoir

Singapore's main territory looks like a diamond-shaped island, although its territory includes surrounding smaller islands. The farthest outlying island is [Pedra Branca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedra_Branca,_Singapore "Pedra Branca, Singapore"). Of Singapore's dozens of smaller islands, [Jurong Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurong_Island "Jurong Island"), [Pulau Tekong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulau_Tekong "Pulau Tekong"), [Pulau Ubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulau_Ubin "Pulau Ubin") and [Sentosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentosa "Sentosa") are the larger ones. Most of Singapore is no more than 15 metres (49 feet) above sea level.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-3)

The highest point of Singapore is [Bukit Timah Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukit_Timah_Hill "Bukit Timah Hill"), with a height from the ground of 164 m (538 ft) and made up of [igneous rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igneous_rock "Igneous rock"), [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite"). Hills and valleys of [sedimentary rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") dominate the northwest, while the eastern region consists of [sandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand "Sand") and flatter land.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:1-4) Singapore has no natural lakes, but reservoirs and [water catchment areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_catchment_area "Water catchment area") have been constructed to store fresh water for [Singapore's water supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_resources_of_Singapore "Water resources of Singapore").

### Land reclamation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Land reclamation")]

Main article: [Land reclamation in Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation_in_Singapore "Land reclamation in Singapore")

Singapore has engaged in extensive [land reclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation_in_Singapore "Land reclamation in Singapore") since the [British colonisation in 1819](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_years_of_modern_Singapore "Founding years of modern Singapore"), using earth sourced from its own hills, the seabed and neighbouring countries.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-5) As a result, the country's land area has expanded from approximately 582 square kilometres (225 sq mi) in the 1960s to around 745 square kilometres (288 sq mi) in the 2020s. Reclamation continues today with the use of newer methods such as [polders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polder "Polder") and [barrages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrage_(dam) "Barrage (dam)") to counter rising sea levels.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-6)

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Climate")]

See also: [Peninsular Malaysian rain forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_Malaysian_rain_forests "Peninsular Malaysian rain forests")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Telok_Ayer_Green_Park_3%2C_Dec_05.JPG/250px-Telok_Ayer_Green_Park_3%2C_Dec_05.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Telok_Ayer_Green_Park_3,_Dec_05.JPG)

Afternoon [thunderstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm") are a frequent occurrence in Singapore, which has an [equatorial climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_climate "Equatorial climate").

Singapore is one-and-a-half degrees north of the equator, lying entirely between the [1st](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_parallel_north "1st parallel north") and [2nd parallels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_parallel_north "2nd parallel north"). Singapore's climate is classified as [tropical rainforest climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_rainforest_climate "Tropical rainforest climate") ([Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")_Af_), with no true distinct seasons. Owing to its geographical location and maritime exposure, its climate is characterised by uniform temperature and pressure, high humidity and abundant rainfall. Therefore, it is almost always warm and wet. The average annual rainfall is around 2,340 mm (92.1 in). The highest 24-hour rainfall figures ever recorded in history were 512.4 mm (20.2 in) (2 December 1978) at [Paya Lebar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paya_Lebar "Paya Lebar"), 467 mm (18.4 in) (1969) and 366 mm (14.4 in) (19 December 2006).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-7) The wettest month on record is January 1893 at 818.6 mm (32.23 in) at the climate station since rainfall records began in 1869, although the wettest ever month of all weather stations across Singapore was in December 2006 at [Buangkok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buangkok "Buangkok") at 996.3 mm (39.22 in).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-8)

The temperature hovers around a [diurnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diurnal_temperature_variation "Diurnal temperature variation") range of a minimum of 25°C (77.0°F) and a maximum of 33°C (91.4°F). May is the hottest month of the year in Singapore, followed by June. This is due to light winds and strong sunshine during those months.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-9) The highest recorded temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), which was recorded twice on 17 April 1983 and 13 May 2023.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-10) The lowest recorded temperature was 19.4°C (66.9°F) on 14 February 1989 at [Paya Lebar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paya_Lebar "Paya Lebar"), although there is an unofficial record low of 18.4°C (65.1°F) on an unspecified date.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-12) At the climate station in [Changi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changi "Changi") however, extremes have ranged from 36.0°C (96.8°F) on 30 March 1998 to 19.4°C (66.9°F) on January 30 and 31 1934.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-www.weather.gov.sg-13) Temperature often goes above 33.2°C (91.8°F) and can reach 35°C (95°F) at times.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-14)

[Relative humidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_humidity "Relative humidity") has a diurnal range in the high 90s in the early morning to around 60% in the mid-afternoon, but does go below 50% at times.During prolonged heavy rain, relative humidity often reaches 100%. Generally, there is much more rainfall on the western side of the island than on the eastern portion of Singapore, owing to a [rain shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow "Rain shadow") effect.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:0-15)

Thus, the eastern side of Singapore is much drier and slightly hotter than western Singapore.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:0-15) This can cause slight weather disparities from one side of the island to the other. This is significant to note because even a small hill such as [Bukit Timah Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukit_Timah_Hill "Bukit Timah Hill") can cause this phenomenon. Despite Singapore's small size, there may be sunshine on one side while there is rain on the other.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Further contrasts that prevent true all-year uniformity are the [monsoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon "Monsoon") seasons which happen twice each year.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The first one is the Northeast Monsoon which occurs from mid-November to early March. The second is the Southwest Monsoon season which occurs from June to September. Periods between monsoon seasons receive less rain and wind. During the Northeast Monsoon, northeast winds [prevail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prevailing_wind "Prevailing wind"), sometimes reach 20 km/h (12 mph). There are cloudy conditions in December and January with frequent afternoon showers.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:0-15)

Spells of widespread moderate to heavy rain occur lasting from 1 to 3 days at a stretch. It is relatively dry in February till early March although rainfall still exceeds 120 mm (4.7 in). It is also generally windy with wind speeds sometimes reaching 30 to 50 km/h (19 to 31 mph) in the months of January and February. During the Southwest Monsoon season, southeast winds prevail. Isolated to scattered showers occur in the late morning and early afternoon. Early morning "[Sumatra Squalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatras "Sumatras")" – [squall lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squall_line "Squall line") that originate over nearby Sumatra– are common.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:0-15)

### Climate change initiatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Climate change initiatives")]

See also: [Climate change in Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_in_Singapore "Climate change in Singapore")

Singapore recognises that [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") in the decades ahead will have major implications for the island-nation. It has taken a three-prong approach to the issue - researching how the nation will be affected in specific details, implementing mitigation measures and adapting to the coming changes. For the research, a Centre for Climate Research Singapore (CCRS) has been established.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-20)

The government estimates that $100 billion will need to be spent over a 100-year time frame to address the issue. In the 2020 budget, it has set aside an initial $5 billion towards a Coastline and Flood Protection Fund.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-21) For the population, it will provide incentives for owners to convert to electric vehicles (EVs), like rebates on the Additional Registration fees and expanding the EV charging network. By 2040, it expects to phase out petrol and diesel (internal combustion engine) vehicles. The country's transport policy continues to focus on a "car-lite" future with most commuters using public transportation ([MRT trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_Rapid_Transit_(Singapore) "Mass Rapid Transit (Singapore)"), buses, taxis) instead. [[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-22)

Singapore is the first country in Southeast Asia to levy a [carbon tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_tax "Carbon tax"), at $5 per ton, applicable for its largest carbon-emitting corporations that produce more than 25,000 tons of carbon dioxide per year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-23) To reduce the country's dependence on fossil fuels, it is building one of the world's largest floating solar farms at Tengeh Reservoir in Tuas, with a capacity of 60MW.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-24)

## Geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Geology")]

Main article: [Geology of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Singapore "Geology of Singapore")

[Igneous rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igneous_rocks "Igneous rocks") are found in [Bukit Timah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukit_Timah "Bukit Timah") and [Woodlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlands,_Singapore "Woodlands, Singapore") and [Pulau Ubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulau_Ubin "Pulau Ubin") island. Granite makes up the bulk of the igneous rock. [Gabbro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabbro "Gabbro") is also found in the area and is found in an area called [Little Guilin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Guilin "Little Guilin") named for its resemblance to Guilin in Southern China. This area is in Bukit Gombak. [Sedimentary rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") are found on the western part of Singapore and is mainly made of [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone") and [mudstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudstone "Mudstone"). It also includes the [southwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_directions "Ordinal directions") area. [Metamorphic rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphic_rock "Metamorphic rock") are found in the [northeastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_direction "Ordinal direction") part of Singapore and also on [Pulau Tekong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulau_Tekong "Pulau Tekong") off the east coast of Singapore. The rocks are mainly made up of [quartzite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartzite "Quartzite") and also make up the Sajahat Formation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:1-4)

### Seismic activity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Seismic activity")]

Singapore is relatively safe from seismic activity in the region, as the nearest major [active faults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_fault "Active fault") (Sumatran fault and Sunda megathrust fault) are hundreds of kilometres away in Indonesia. However, the population and buildings are prone to being only very slightly affected by any activity as tremors, which is not uncommon, but generally does not do any harm and is limited to small amounts of swaying or vibration of objects.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:2-26)

In late 2004, several parts of Asia and Africa were struck by the [2004 Indian Ocean earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake "2004 Indian Ocean earthquake") and the resulting tsunami. Singapore was fortunate as it was protected by the [Sumatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatra "Sumatra") landmass, which bore the brunt of the tsunami; the effect on Singapore was limited to tremors felt in some of the common high-rise buildings there.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:2-26)

## Political and human

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Political and human")]

Main articles: [Administrative divisions of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_divisions_of_Singapore "Administrative divisions of Singapore") and [List of places in Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_places_in_Singapore "List of places in Singapore")

See also: [Regions of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_Singapore "Regions of Singapore"), [Planning Areas of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_Areas_of_Singapore "Planning Areas of Singapore"), and [New towns of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_towns_of_Singapore "New towns of Singapore")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Toa_Payoh_New_Town%2C_Toa_Payoh_Lorong_6_2%2C_Jan_06.JPG/250px-Toa_Payoh_New_Town%2C_Toa_Payoh_Lorong_6_2%2C_Jan_06.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Toa_Payoh_New_Town,_Toa_Payoh_Lorong_6_2,_Jan_06.JPG)

Singapore's urban geography is often characterised by extensive use of [HDB flats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_housing_in_Singapore "Public housing in Singapore"), which the majority of citizens reside in.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Singapore2021OSM.png/250px-Singapore2021OSM.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Singapore2021OSM.png)

Enlargeable, detailed map of Singapore

When Singapore was first colonised by the British, the [City of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Singapore_(historical_entity) "City of Singapore (historical entity)") was situated on the southern coast, around the mouth of the [Singapore River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_River "Singapore River").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-27) This area remains the [Central Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Area,_Singapore "Central Area, Singapore") of Singapore. The rest of the island was [farmland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmland_(farming) "Farmland (farming)") and primary [rainforest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforest "Rainforest"). Since the 1960s, the government has constructed [new towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_towns_of_Singapore "New towns of Singapore") in other areas, so that today the island is nearly entirely built-up and [urbanised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanised "Urbanised"), with only a few exceptions.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The country has several subdivisions, mostly used for administrative or statistical purposes. Politically, Singapore is divided into five administrative districts, these are then further subdivided into [town councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_council#Singapore "Town council") which usually consists of one or more [political constituencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituencies_of_Singapore "Constituencies of Singapore"). Planning and census boundaries, called [planning areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_Areas_of_Singapore "Planning Areas of Singapore"), have been used by the [Urban Redevelopment Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Redevelopment_Authority "Urban Redevelopment Authority") to define certain districts and neighbourhoods.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-28)

There are two connections to the state of [Johor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johor "Johor"), Malaysia. In the north there is a [causeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johor%E2%80%93Singapore_Causeway "Johor–Singapore Causeway") for both rail and road traffic, which connects to the city of [Johor Bahru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johor_Bahru "Johor Bahru"). In the west there is a road bridge ([Tuas Second Link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia%E2%80%93Singapore_Second_Link "Malaysia–Singapore Second Link")), which connects to Johor, for road traffic only.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-30)

There are more than 300 parks and 4 nature reserves in Singapore. There are also many trees planted, and almost fifty per cent of the country is covered by greenery. Because of this, Singapore is also commonly known as the 'Garden City'.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-31)

Singapore remains highly vulnerable to the [impact of climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_of_climate_change "Effects of climate change"); in particular, the rising sea levels may pose a major threat to the very survival of the country in the long-term perspective.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-32)

[Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") is a [city-state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-state "City-state") and [island country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_country "Island country") in [maritime Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_Southeast_Asia "Maritime Southeast Asia"), located at the end of the [Malayan Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayan_Peninsula "Malayan Peninsula") between [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia") and [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia") as well as the [Straits of Malacca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Malacca "Straits of Malacca") and the [South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea"). It is highly compact and urbanised. As of 2026, Singapore has a total land area of approximately 744.3 square kilometres (287.4 sq mi).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-total_area_of_Singapore-1) Singapore is separated from Indonesia by the [Singapore Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_Strait "Singapore Strait") and from Malaysia by the [Straits of Johor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Johor "Straits of Johor").

Geographically, Singapore comprises its [mainland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_Island "Singapore Island") and other islands. The mainland of Singapore measures 50 kilometres (31 mi) from east to west and 27 kilometres (17 mi) from north to south with 193 kilometres (120 mi) of coastline. These figures are based on 2.515 metres (8 ft 3.0 in) High Water Mark [cadastral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadastre "Cadastre") survey boundaries.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-Department_of_Statistics_Singapore-2) It has an [exclusive economic zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclusive_economic_zone "Exclusive economic zone") of 1,067 km 2 (412 mi 2).

## Topography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Topography")]

See also: [List of islands of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Singapore "List of islands of Singapore") and [Extreme points of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_points_of_Singapore "Extreme points of Singapore")

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Upper_Seletar_Reservoir_5%2C_Oct_05.JPG/250px-Upper_Seletar_Reservoir_5%2C_Oct_05.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Seletar_Reservoir_5,_Oct_05.JPG)

Upper Seletar Reservoir

Singapore's main territory looks like a diamond-shaped island, although its territory includes surrounding smaller islands. The farthest outlying island is [Pedra Branca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedra_Branca,_Singapore "Pedra Branca, Singapore"). Of Singapore's dozens of smaller islands, [Jurong Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurong_Island "Jurong Island"), [Pulau Tekong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulau_Tekong "Pulau Tekong"), [Pulau Ubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulau_Ubin "Pulau Ubin") and [Sentosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentosa "Sentosa") are the larger ones. Most of Singapore is no more than 15 metres (49 feet) above sea level.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-3)

The highest point of Singapore is [Bukit Timah Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukit_Timah_Hill "Bukit Timah Hill"), with a height from the ground of 164 m (538 ft) and made up of [igneous rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igneous_rock "Igneous rock"), [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite"). Hills and valleys of [sedimentary rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") dominate the northwest, while the eastern region consists of [sandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand "Sand") and flatter land.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:1-4) Singapore has no natural lakes, but reservoirs and [water catchment areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_catchment_area "Water catchment area") have been constructed to store fresh water for [Singapore's water supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_resources_of_Singapore "Water resources of Singapore").

### Land reclamation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Land reclamation")]

Main article: [Land reclamation in Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation_in_Singapore "Land reclamation in Singapore")

Singapore has engaged in extensive [land reclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation_in_Singapore "Land reclamation in Singapore") since the [British colonisation in 1819](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_years_of_modern_Singapore "Founding years of modern Singapore"), using earth sourced from its own hills, the seabed and neighbouring countries.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-5) As a result, the country's land area has expanded from approximately 582 square kilometres (225 sq mi) in the 1960s to around 745 square kilometres (288 sq mi) in the 2020s. Reclamation continues today with the use of newer methods such as [polders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polder "Polder") and [barrages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrage_(dam) "Barrage (dam)") to counter rising sea levels.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-6)

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Climate")]

See also: [Peninsular Malaysian rain forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_Malaysian_rain_forests "Peninsular Malaysian rain forests")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Telok_Ayer_Green_Park_3%2C_Dec_05.JPG/250px-Telok_Ayer_Green_Park_3%2C_Dec_05.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Telok_Ayer_Green_Park_3,_Dec_05.JPG)

Afternoon [thunderstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm") are a frequent occurrence in Singapore, which has an [equatorial climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_climate "Equatorial climate").

Singapore is one-and-a-half degrees north of the equator, lying entirely between the [1st](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_parallel_north "1st parallel north") and [2nd parallels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_parallel_north "2nd parallel north"). Singapore's climate is classified as [tropical rainforest climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_rainforest_climate "Tropical rainforest climate") ([Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")_Af_), with no true distinct seasons. Owing to its geographical location and maritime exposure, its climate is characterised by uniform temperature and pressure, high humidity and abundant rainfall. Therefore, it is almost always warm and wet. The average annual rainfall is around 2,340 mm (92.1 in). The highest 24-hour rainfall figures ever recorded in history were 512.4 mm (20.2 in) (2 December 1978) at [Paya Lebar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paya_Lebar "Paya Lebar"), 467 mm (18.4 in) (1969) and 366 mm (14.4 in) (19 December 2006).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-7) The wettest month on record is January 1893 at 818.6 mm (32.23 in) at the climate station since rainfall records began in 1869, although the wettest ever month of all weather stations across Singapore was in December 2006 at [Buangkok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buangkok "Buangkok") at 996.3 mm (39.22 in).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-8)

The temperature hovers around a [diurnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diurnal_temperature_variation "Diurnal temperature variation") range of a minimum of 25°C (77.0°F) and a maximum of 33°C (91.4°F). May is the hottest month of the year in Singapore, followed by June. This is due to light winds and strong sunshine during those months.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-9) The highest recorded temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), which was recorded twice on 17 April 1983 and 13 May 2023.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-10) The lowest recorded temperature was 19.4°C (66.9°F) on 14 February 1989 at [Paya Lebar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paya_Lebar "Paya Lebar"), although there is an unofficial record low of 18.4°C (65.1°F) on an unspecified date.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-12) At the climate station in [Changi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changi "Changi") however, extremes have ranged from 36.0°C (96.8°F) on 30 March 1998 to 19.4°C (66.9°F) on January 30 and 31 1934.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-www.weather.gov.sg-13) Temperature often goes above 33.2°C (91.8°F) and can reach 35°C (95°F) at times.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-14)

[Relative humidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_humidity "Relative humidity") has a diurnal range in the high 90s in the early morning to around 60% in the mid-afternoon, but does go below 50% at times.During prolonged heavy rain, relative humidity often reaches 100%. Generally, there is much more rainfall on the western side of the island than on the eastern portion of Singapore, owing to a [rain shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow "Rain shadow") effect.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:0-15)

Thus, the eastern side of Singapore is much drier and slightly hotter than western Singapore.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:0-15) This can cause slight weather disparities from one side of the island to the other. This is significant to note because even a small hill such as [Bukit Timah Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukit_Timah_Hill "Bukit Timah Hill") can cause this phenomenon. Despite Singapore's small size, there may be sunshine on one side while there is rain on the other.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Further contrasts that prevent true all-year uniformity are the [monsoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon "Monsoon") seasons which happen twice each year.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The first one is the Northeast Monsoon which occurs from mid-November to early March. The second is the Southwest Monsoon season which occurs from June to September. Periods between monsoon seasons receive less rain and wind. During the Northeast Monsoon, northeast winds [prevail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prevailing_wind "Prevailing wind"), sometimes reach 20 km/h (12 mph). There are cloudy conditions in December and January with frequent afternoon showers.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:0-15)

Spells of widespread moderate to heavy rain occur lasting from 1 to 3 days at a stretch. It is relatively dry in February till early March although rainfall still exceeds 120 mm (4.7 in). It is also generally windy with wind speeds sometimes reaching 30 to 50 km/h (19 to 31 mph) in the months of January and February. During the Southwest Monsoon season, southeast winds prevail. Isolated to scattered showers occur in the late morning and early afternoon. Early morning "[Sumatra Squalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatras "Sumatras")" – [squall lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squall_line "Squall line") that originate over nearby Sumatra– are common.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:0-15)

### Climate change initiatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Climate change initiatives")]

See also: [Climate change in Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_in_Singapore "Climate change in Singapore")

Singapore recognises that [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") in the decades ahead will have major implications for the island-nation. It has taken a three-prong approach to the issue - researching how the nation will be affected in specific details, implementing mitigation measures and adapting to the coming changes. For the research, a Centre for Climate Research Singapore (CCRS) has been established.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-20)

The government estimates that $100 billion will need to be spent over a 100-year time frame to address the issue. In the 2020 budget, it has set aside an initial $5 billion towards a Coastline and Flood Protection Fund.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-21) For the population, it will provide incentives for owners to convert to electric vehicles (EVs), like rebates on the Additional Registration fees and expanding the EV charging network. By 2040, it expects to phase out petrol and diesel (internal combustion engine) vehicles. The country's transport policy continues to focus on a "car-lite" future with most commuters using public transportation ([MRT trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_Rapid_Transit_(Singapore) "Mass Rapid Transit (Singapore)"), buses, taxis) instead. [[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-22)

Singapore is the first country in Southeast Asia to levy a [carbon tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_tax "Carbon tax"), at $5 per ton, applicable for its largest carbon-emitting corporations that produce more than 25,000 tons of carbon dioxide per year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-23) To reduce the country's dependence on fossil fuels, it is building one of the world's largest floating solar farms at Tengeh Reservoir in Tuas, with a capacity of 60MW.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-24)

## Geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Geology")]

Main article: [Geology of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Singapore "Geology of Singapore")

[![Image 8: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. [Igneous rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igneous_rocks "Igneous rocks") are found in [Bukit Timah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukit_Timah "Bukit Timah") and [Woodlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlands,_Singapore "Woodlands, Singapore") and [Pulau Ubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulau_Ubin "Pulau Ubin") island. Granite makes up the bulk of the igneous rock. [Gabbro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabbro "Gabbro") is also found in the area and is found in an area called [Little Guilin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Guilin "Little Guilin") named for its resemblance to Guilin in Southern China. This area is in Bukit Gombak. [Sedimentary rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") are found on the western part of Singapore and is mainly made of [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone") and [mudstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudstone "Mudstone"). It also includes the [southwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_directions "Ordinal directions") area. [Metamorphic rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphic_rock "Metamorphic rock") are found in the [northeastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_direction "Ordinal direction") part of Singapore and also on [Pulau Tekong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulau_Tekong "Pulau Tekong") off the east coast of Singapore. The rocks are mainly made up of [quartzite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartzite "Quartzite") and also make up the Sajahat Formation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:1-4)

### Seismic activity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Seismic activity")]

Singapore is relatively safe from seismic activity in the region, as the nearest major [active faults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_fault "Active fault") (Sumatran fault and Sunda megathrust fault) are hundreds of kilometres away in Indonesia. However, the population and buildings are prone to being only very slightly affected by any activity as tremors, which is not uncommon, but generally does not do any harm and is limited to small amounts of swaying or vibration of objects.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:2-26)

In late 2004, several parts of Asia and Africa were struck by the [2004 Indian Ocean earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake "2004 Indian Ocean earthquake") and the resulting tsunami. Singapore was fortunate as it was protected by the [Sumatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatra "Sumatra") landmass, which bore the brunt of the tsunami; the effect on Singapore was limited to tremors felt in some of the common high-rise buildings there.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-:2-26)

## Political and human

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geography_of_Singapore&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Political and human")]

Main articles: [Administrative divisions of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_divisions_of_Singapore "Administrative divisions of Singapore") and [List of places in Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_places_in_Singapore "List of places in Singapore")

See also: [Regions of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_Singapore "Regions of Singapore"), [Planning Areas of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_Areas_of_Singapore "Planning Areas of Singapore"), and [New towns of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_towns_of_Singapore "New towns of Singapore")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Toa_Payoh_New_Town%2C_Toa_Payoh_Lorong_6_2%2C_Jan_06.JPG/250px-Toa_Payoh_New_Town%2C_Toa_Payoh_Lorong_6_2%2C_Jan_06.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Toa_Payoh_New_Town,_Toa_Payoh_Lorong_6_2,_Jan_06.JPG)

Singapore's urban geography is often characterised by extensive use of [HDB flats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_housing_in_Singapore "Public housing in Singapore"), which the majority of citizens reside in.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Singapore2021OSM.png/250px-Singapore2021OSM.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Singapore2021OSM.png)

Enlargeable, detailed map of Singapore

When Singapore was first colonised by the British, the [City of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Singapore_(historical_entity) "City of Singapore (historical entity)") was situated on the southern coast, around the mouth of the [Singapore River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_River "Singapore River").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-27) This area remains the [Central Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Area,_Singapore "Central Area, Singapore") of Singapore. The rest of the island was [farmland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmland_(farming) "Farmland (farming)") and primary [rainforest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforest "Rainforest"). Since the 1960s, the government has constructed [new towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_towns_of_Singapore "New towns of Singapore") in other areas, so that today the island is nearly entirely built-up and [urbanised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanised "Urbanised"), with only a few exceptions.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The country has several subdivisions, mostly used for administrative or statistical purposes. Politically, Singapore is divided into five administrative districts, these are then further subdivided into [town councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_council#Singapore "Town council") which usually consists of one or more [political constituencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituencies_of_Singapore "Constituencies of Singapore"). Planning and census boundaries, called [planning areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_Areas_of_Singapore "Planning Areas of Singapore"), have been used by the [Urban Redevelopment Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Redevelopment_Authority "Urban Redevelopment Authority") to define certain districts and neighbourhoods.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-28)

There are two connections to the state of [Johor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johor "Johor"), Malaysia. In the north there is a [causeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johor%E2%80%93Singapore_Causeway "Johor–Singapore Causeway") for both rail and road traffic, which connects to the city of [Johor Bahru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johor_Bahru "Johor Bahru"). In the west there is a road bridge ([Tuas Second Link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia%E2%80%93Singapore_Second_Link "Malaysia–Singapore Second Link")), which connects to Johor, for road traffic only.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-30)

There are more than 300 parks and 4 nature reserves in Singapore. There are also many trees planted, and almost fifty per cent of the country is covered by greenery. Because of this, Singapore is also commonly known as the 'Garden City'.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-31)

Singapore remains highly vulnerable to the [impact of climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_of_climate_change "Effects of climate change"); in particular, the rising sea levels may pose a major threat to the very survival of the country in the long-term perspective.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Singapore#cite_note-32)

# Where is Singapore?

Singapore has a well-earned reputation as a multicultural nation with strict laws and a powerful economy, but not everyone can point to it on a map. So where is Singapore?

**Singapore is located in Southeast Asia and is part of the Asian continent.**

### Singapore Interesting Facts
