*   #### Michaels, Albert '55 - July 26

Michaels, Albert L.  
Jun. 20, 1937 - Jul. 26, 2026  
  
Dr. Albert L. Michaels, a renowned history professor who spent  
more than 50 years in the classroom and whose courses on a  
variety of subjects, including terrorism, U.S. foreign policy and  
Latin America, remained popular over several generations of  
students, died on July 26, 2026. He was 89.  
Outside teaching, Dr. Michaels emerged as a leading expert on  
Western New York art, writing books and articles and curating  
exhibits that helped draw attention to the region’s rich but often  
overlooked contribution to the history of American art in the 20th  
Century.  
But it was in the classroom where Dr. Michaels dedicated most of  
his time and energy. He was single-minded in his devotion to  
teaching and was constantly innovating to engage students, said  
his colleague Dr. York Norman, who co-taught a class with him on  
terrorism at Buffalo State.  
“He did research, he wrote,” Dr. Norman said. “But it was teaching  
he focused on.”  
Dr. Michaels had been at University at Buffalo for more than 40  
years—a familiar figure around campus with his signature bow  
ties, round glasses and unruly head of gray hair—when he left for  
a job at Buffalo State College in 2009, citing the lack of emphasis  
on teaching undergraduates as well as the lack of ideological  
diversity as his reasons for leaving.  
He went on to teach at Buffalo State for about another ten years  
before retiring. “He was really active,” Dr. Norman said. “He went on working until  
he couldn’t anymore.”  
A conservative provocateur who enjoyed tweaking his more  
liberal colleagues, Dr. Michaels was no ideological purist. He  
encouraged his students to think independently and challenge  
orthodoxy, as he himself did.  
During the tumult of the late 1960s, when clouds of tear gas  
drifted across campus, his classes were popular among members  
of the Students for a Democratic Society, the radical anti-war  
group. The SDS students, he once said, welcomed the  
opportunity to have their views challenged in the classroom in an  
atmosphere of mutual respect and Dr. Michaels said he enjoyed  
getting to know them.  
He had challenged conservative orthodoxy in other ways. He  
struck up a friendship with Orlando Letelier, the Chilean leftist  
leader, and played a role in getting him released from a  
concentration camp in Chile, where he was being held by the  
regime of dictator Augusto Pinochet. Letelier was later  
assassinated in Washington by agents of Pinochet’s regime.  
Dr. Michaels was born in 1937, in Buffalo, the youngest of three  
children of Phyllis and Dewey Michaels. His father owned and  
operated the Palace Theater, a famed burlesque venue that  
closed its doors in 1967.  
He attended Nichols School and then the University of  
Pennsylvania, where he earned an undergraduate degree and a  
Ph.D in Latin American history.  
He taught and wrote extensively about Latin America, but over the  
years expanded his course offerings to include classes on the John F. Kennedy assassination, the Cold War and the media,  
among other subjects that interested him.  
At the same time, he delved into the world of regional art,  
authoring books on 20th Century painters Alexander Levy and  
Virginia Cuthbert and on Buffalo architecture. He was behind a  
number of major exhibits at the Burchfield Penney Art Center,  
where he served as an adviser and co-curator.  
He steered the center toward major acquisitions and helped  
attract the funding to build Burchfield Penney’s current home, said  
Scott Propeack, the center’s executive director.  
“The lasting impact that Albie had on our institution and the  
collections of many prominent Buffalo collectors has been  
defining,” Mr. Propeack said.  
Dr. Michaels personally amassed a vast art collection over the  
years and paintings and sculptures filled every inch of his  
apartment on Delaware Ave. Canvases were stacked deep  
against the walls and on every piece of furniture so that visitors  
had to clear a place before they could sit, where they were often  
joined by his energetic Jack Russell Terrier, Mack.  
He enjoyed his reputation as a conservative firebrand, but those  
who knew him understood he didn’t take his role too seriously  
“He loved to get people agitated,” Dr. Norman said.  
That sometimes drove his colleagues nuts, but his students  
seemed to enjoy his candor and many respected his refusal to  
coddle their sensitivities.  
One student, Greg Pavlov, who took a course from Dr. Michaels  
more than 50 years ago, still remembers vigorous debates in his class and how he always encouraged alternative views and  
respected them.  
“If you have been weaned on a diet of liberal politics and ideology,  
Dr. Michaels’ class will doubtless be an eye opener,” another  
student wrote on social media. “His grading is tough and there are  
those who seem to resent the debasement of their high-school  
ideology, but in time they grow up and realize how much sense  
his classes make.”  
He is survived by his sons, George Michaels, of Edgartown,  
Mass., and Wilkinson Michaels, of Buffalo, N.Y. , and his  
grandchildren, James, Emily and Edward.  
The family will be present Saturday, August 8, 2026 from 11 AM-  
12 PM at the (Amherst Chapel) AMIGONE FUNERAL HOME,  
INC. 5200 Sheridan Dr. (at Hopkins Rd), where a Funeral Service  
will follow at 12 PM. Memorial contributions may be made to  
Petfinder. Share condolences at [www.AMIGONE.com](https://www.nicholsschool.org/alumni/www.AMIGONE.com)

He grew up on Lincoln Parkway, in the bosom of Buffalo’s mid-century high society. He was an usher at numerous debutante balls and hosted sports parties at his family's summer home in Clarksburg in the Town of Eden, which his grandfather Dr. James Lewis had built.  
      He was a 1952 graduate of Nichols School, where he was captain of the track team, and followed his older brother James to Dartmouth College. He majored in English and was a member of Theta Delta Chi fraternity. He completed his law degree at the University at Buffalo. When he was admitted to the bar in 1962, he joined his father and brother James in Magavern, Lowe and Beilwech, the city's oldest law firm. Now Magavern Magavern Grimm LLP, its roots trace back to 1826. He was the firm's senior counsel.   Mr. Magavern ventured into preservation in 1963 when he and a partner bought one of Buffalo's earliest luxury apartment buildings, designed by architect E. B. Green and built on North Street during World War I.     Two years later, as vice president of the Allentown Association, which he helped establish, he was in the forefront of efforts to preserve the Wilcox Mansion on Delaware Avenue, where President Theodore Roosevelt was sworn in, and designate it as a historic site.  
    In the late 1960s, he joined with a group of businessmen to organize the Johnson Park Restoration Corp., which bought 14 vandalized 19th century homes at the edge of downtown Buffalo and revitalized them. He was the company's secretary.   "Contracts were out for their demolition. We felt the whole West Side could go if Johnson Park did," he told Buffalo News reporter Karen Brady when she wrote about the park's rebirth in 1986. “We felt it was an important anchor for Elmwood Avenue, a link between Allentown and downtown. ## 2026

### List of 26 items.

*   #### Becker Jr., Max '46 - January 22

Max Becker Jr. of Buffalo passed away peacefully on January 22, 2026, at age 97, at home, in the presence of family. He is reunited with the love of his life and wife of 60 years, Cora Hunt Dickinson, who passed in 2010. Max was born in 1928 and attended Nichols School, graduated from Phillips Andover Academy and after graduation from Amherst College in 1950, joined his father at the Buffalo real estate and insurance firm Gurney Becker & Bourne. In October 1950 he married his soulmate, Cora H. Dickinson (Corky). Nine months later, in July 1950, he was activated as part of Headquarters and Headquarters Battery 209 Antiaircraft Artillery Group and served in the Korean War. He and Corky moved to Georgia where Max trained at Camp Gordon, GA; Camp Stewart, GA; and Indiantown Gap Military Reservation. He was deactivated in August 1952 as Master Sargeant. He returned with Corky to Buffalo and resumed his employment with Gurney Becker & Bourne, and his distinguished career in real estate and general insurance. Until November 2025 and for over 70 years prior, he worked at Gurney Becker & Bourne, most recently serving as Chairman. Initially, he worked in residential real estate and insurance. He later changed to include commercial and industrial real estate to his main area of expertise. *   #### Hoyt, Austin '55 - July 17

Austin Hoyt, a longtime television producer from South Dartmouth, Massachusetts, died on July 17 from complications of coronary heart disease.  
  
Born Herbert Austin Aikins Hoyt in Buffalo, New York, on June 20, 1937, he attended Nichols School and The Hill School before graduating from Yale University in 1959.  
  
Hoyt joined WGBH in 1965 and remained there for 38 years, followed by seven more as an independent producer.  
  
Hoyt began his career as a reporter for the Niagara Falls Gazette, then worked on WGBH's first local news program before spending two years at Public Broadcast Laboratory, where he produced the environmental documentary "Multiply and Subdue the Earth." He helped create The Advocates in 1969 and served as executive producer of ZOOM in 1974. His body of work includes "LBJ Goes to War," which won an Emmy and a Writers Guild Award, and the acclaimed series Vietnam: A Television History. He earned Peabody Awards for "Crisis in Central America," "Ike"; and 'Reagan," along with a primetime Emmy in 1999 for his biography of Douglas MacArthur. His 2005 program "Victory in the Pacific," a personal favorite, received three Emmy nominations.  
  
Historian David McCullough once counted Hoyt among the finest documentary filmmakers of historical documentaries and biographies of the era, citing his film on Andrew Carnegie, "The Richest Man in the World."  
  
“Austin Hoyt was one of the reasons Boston's PBS station WGBH grew from a regional educational television station in 1969 to the national public television powerhouse it is today,” said Peter McGhee, WGBH’s manager of national programming.  
  
An avid paddler, Hoyt led notable expeditions including a 1959 ascent of the South Nahanni River and a 1962 descent of the Back River to the Arctic Ocean, the first since the nineteenth century. He later authored two books: a 2011 oral history of Bill Levitt and, in 2025, an account of his Nahanni River journey. He was also a devoted sailor and skier, serving for decades on the management committee at Utah's Snowbird resort.  
  
He met Felicity Forbes at the Alta Lodge in 2000 and married her in 2004, building a life together in South Dartmouth.  He was predeceased by his parents, three sisters, and his twin brother. He is survived by his wife, Felicity; her children and grandchildren; several nieces, nephews, and their families; and a stepson.  
  
A life celebration will be held on September 12. Donations in Austin’s memory may be made to The WGBH Educational Foundation or the Dartmouth Natural Resources Trust (DNRT).

*   #### Michaels, Albert '55 - July 26

Michaels, Albert L.  
Jun. 20, 1937 - Jul. 26, 2026  
  
Dr. Albert L. Michaels, a renowned history professor who spent  
more than 50 years in the classroom and whose courses on a  
variety of subjects, including terrorism, U.S. foreign policy and  
Latin America, remained popular over several generations of  
students, died on July 26, 2026. He was 89.  
Outside teaching, Dr. Michaels emerged as a leading expert on  
Western New York art, writing books and articles and curating  
exhibits that helped draw attention to the region’s rich but often  
overlooked contribution to the history of American art in the 20th  
Century.  
But it was in the classroom where Dr. Michaels dedicated most of  
his time and energy. He was single-minded in his devotion to  
teaching and was constantly innovating to engage students, said  
his colleague Dr. York Norman, who co-taught a class with him on  
terrorism at Buffalo State.  
“He did research, he wrote,” Dr. Norman said. “But it was teaching  
he focused on.”  
Dr. Michaels had been at University at Buffalo for more than 40  
years—a familiar figure around campus with his signature bow  
ties, round glasses and unruly head of gray hair—when he left for  
a job at Buffalo State College in 2009, citing the lack of emphasis  
on teaching undergraduates as well as the lack of ideological  
diversity as his reasons for leaving.  
He went on to teach at Buffalo State for about another ten years  
before retiring. “He was really active,” Dr. Norman said. “He went on working until  
he couldn’t anymore.”  
A conservative provocateur who enjoyed tweaking his more  
liberal colleagues, Dr. Michaels was no ideological purist. He  
encouraged his students to think independently and challenge  
orthodoxy, as he himself did.  
During the tumult of the late 1960s, when clouds of tear gas  
drifted across campus, his classes were popular among members  
of the Students for a Democratic Society, the radical anti-war  
group. The SDS students, he once said, welcomed the  
opportunity to have their views challenged in the classroom in an  
atmosphere of mutual respect and Dr. Michaels said he enjoyed  
getting to know them.  
He had challenged conservative orthodoxy in other ways. He  
struck up a friendship with Orlando Letelier, the Chilean leftist  
leader, and played a role in getting him released from a  
concentration camp in Chile, where he was being held by the  
regime of dictator Augusto Pinochet. Letelier was later  
assassinated in Washington by agents of Pinochet’s regime.  
Dr. Michaels was born in 1937, in Buffalo, the youngest of three  
children of Phyllis and Dewey Michaels. His father owned and  
operated the Palace Theater, a famed burlesque venue that  
closed its doors in 1967.  
He attended Nichols School and then the University of  
Pennsylvania, where he earned an undergraduate degree and a  
Ph.D in Latin American history.  
He taught and wrote extensively about Latin America, but over the  
years expanded his course offerings to include classes on the John F. Kennedy assassination, the Cold War and the media,  
among other subjects that interested him.  
At the same time, he delved into the world of regional art,  
authoring books on 20th Century painters Alexander Levy and  
Virginia Cuthbert and on Buffalo architecture. He was behind a  
number of major exhibits at the Burchfield Penney Art Center,  
where he served as an adviser and co-curator.  
He steered the center toward major acquisitions and helped  
attract the funding to build Burchfield Penney’s current home, said  
Scott Propeack, the center’s executive director.  
“The lasting impact that Albie had on our institution and the  
collections of many prominent Buffalo collectors has been  
defining,” Mr. Propeack said.  
Dr. Michaels personally amassed a vast art collection over the  
years and paintings and sculptures filled every inch of his  
apartment on Delaware Ave. Canvases were stacked deep  
against the walls and on every piece of furniture so that visitors  
had to clear a place before they could sit, where they were often  
joined by his energetic Jack Russell Terrier, Mack.  
He enjoyed his reputation as a conservative firebrand, but those  
who knew him understood he didn’t take his role too seriously  
“He loved to get people agitated,” Dr. Norman said.  
That sometimes drove his colleagues nuts, but his students  
seemed to enjoy his candor and many respected his refusal to  
coddle their sensitivities.  
One student, Greg Pavlov, who took a course from Dr. Michaels  
more than 50 years ago, still remembers vigorous debates in his class and how he always encouraged alternative views and  
respected them.  
“If you have been weaned on a diet of liberal politics and ideology,  
Dr. Michaels’ class will doubtless be an eye opener,” another  
student wrote on social media. “His grading is tough and there are  
those who seem to resent the debasement of their high-school  
ideology, but in time they grow up and realize how much sense  
his classes make.”  
He is survived by his sons, George Michaels, of Edgartown,  
Mass., and Wilkinson Michaels, of Buffalo, N.Y. , and his  
grandchildren, James, Emily and Edward.  
The family will be present Saturday, August 8, 2026 from 11 AM-  
12 PM at the (Amherst Chapel) AMIGONE FUNERAL HOME,  
INC. 5200 Sheridan Dr. (at Hopkins Rd), where a Funeral Service  
will follow at 12 PM. Memorial contributions may be made to  
Petfinder. Share condolences at [www.AMIGONE.com](https://www.nicholsschool.org/alumni/www.AMIGONE.com)

*   #### Empson, George Raymond 'Ray' III '55 - April 29

George Raymond "Ray" Empson III, beloved husband, father, friend, and leader, passed away peacefully on April 29, 2025, in Stamford, Connecticut. He was 87.

By the time he graduated from Nichols School in Buffalo, New York, in 1955, he had earned numerous academic and athletic awards, including nine varsity letters, and had set school records that would stand for decades. In recognition of his achievements, he was inducted into Nichols School's Athletic Hall of Fame in 2023.  
Ray went on to attend Princeton University, where he graduated in 1959 with a degree in English. At Princeton, despite weighing just 140-lbs, he was a standout member of the football and track teams, earning seven letters and placement on the All Ivy League Scholastic Football Team. While his claim to have been offered a tryout with the Cleveland Browns was not able to be confirmed by the time of publication, he was nonetheless remembered by teammates and friends for his grit, determination and speed.  
Following his undergraduate studies, Mr. Empson served in the Army Reserve and earned his law degree from Harvard in 1962. His career began with positions at Milbank, Tweed, Hadley & McCloy - where he represented the New York Stock Exchange and the Rockefeller Family - and the Department of Commerce in Washington, D.C. He later transitioned into finance at Chemical Bank, ultimately rising into a number of senior leadership positions, including Chief Financial Officer of Buster Brown Apparel, as well as President and CEO of Gerber Childrenswear, Alexander Julian and Bike Athletic.  
After leaving the for-profit sector, Mr. Empson would have a long and successful "second career," dedicated to public-minded service in leadership roles at non-profit organizations. He spent the ensuing years promoting conservation and environmental education as the President of Keep America Beautiful and as Chairman of the Arbor Day Foundation, before going on to serve as the President of the SeriousFun Children's Network, the global community of camps and programs for children living with serious illnesses.  
A long-time resident of Darien and New Canaan, Ray was a volunteer coach for youth sports teams and other local organizations, and was a regular at local golf courses. He is survived by his loving wife of 46 years, Gay Morris Empson; his brother, Walter Empson; sons, Josh and Rip Empson; daughter-in-law, Rachel Klauber-Speiden; and grandchildren, Lucinda and Becket Empson-Speiden.  
A true gentleman to the end, Ray's enduring warmth, kindness and grace will be missed by all who knew and loved him, and will be remembered always.  
A memorial service will be held at a later date. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to the Arbor Day Foundation in honor of Ray's enduring commitment to environmental stewardship.

*   #### Magavern II, William J. '52 - April 15

_July 29, 1934 – April 15, 2025_  William J. Magavern II made a proposition to Buffalo State College president Muriel A. Howard in 1998 that was too generous to refuse.  
    A member of the college’s foundation and former chairman, he thought the Burchfield Penney Art Center, then housed in Rockwell Hall, should have its own building. To get it started, he offered a major donation – $1 million.  
    He had three conditions. It needed to be built on Elmwood Avenue. It should be close to the Buffalo State campus. And it must be beautiful.  
    It was the first step in a 10-year process that resulted in a stunning new structure designed by Gwathmey Siegel and Associates across from the Buffalo AKG Art Museum. Mr. Magavern played a major role in raising additional funds for it and creating the design.   An attorney who also was prominent as a preservationist, he died April 15 at his home in Buffalo. He was 90.Watercolor artist Rita Argen Auerbach called him "Burchfield's angel."  
    The son of attorney Samuel Magavern and Gertrude Lewis Magavern, he was introduced to the legal world with a summer job in his father’s office at the age of 14, filing and running errands.  He grew up on Lincoln Parkway, in the bosom of Buffalo’s mid-century high society. He was an usher at numerous debutante balls and hosted sports parties at his family's summer home in Clarksburg in the Town of Eden, which his grandfather Dr. James Lewis had built.  
      He was a 1952 graduate of Nichols School, where he was captain of the track team, and followed his older brother James to Dartmouth College. He majored in English and was a member of Theta Delta Chi fraternity.   Athletic and adventurous, he and a friend spent the summer before his junior year driving to Alaska in a Jeep, stopping along the way to earn money by working on a dam project and harvesting crops in Montana.  
    Mr. Magavern served two years in the Army, was stationed in Germany and returned to attend Cornell University Law School, marrying the mother of his three daughters, Susan J. Clark, in 1960.  He completed his law degree at the University at Buffalo. When he was admitted to the bar in 1962, he joined his father and brother James in Magavern, Lowe and Beilwech, the city's oldest law firm. Now Magavern Magavern Grimm LLP, its roots trace back to 1826. He was the firm's senior counsel.   Mr. Magavern ventured into preservation in 1963 when he and a partner bought one of Buffalo's earliest luxury apartment buildings, designed by architect E. B. Green and built on North Street during World War I.     Two years later, as vice president of the Allentown Association, which he helped establish, he was in the forefront of efforts to preserve the Wilcox Mansion on Delaware Avenue, where President Theodore Roosevelt was sworn in, and designate it as a historic site.  
    In the late 1960s, he joined with a group of businessmen to organize the Johnson Park Restoration Corp., which bought 14 vandalized 19th century homes at the edge of downtown Buffalo and revitalized them. He was the company's secretary.   "Contracts were out for their demolition. We felt the whole West Side could go if Johnson Park did," he told Buffalo News reporter Karen Brady when she wrote about the park's rebirth in 1986. “We felt it was an important anchor for Elmwood Avenue, a link between Allentown and downtown. Now when I see the rehabilitation on Whitney Place and Prospect Avenue, I have a good feeling. I feel it may not be happening without the saving of Johnson Park."   He also became active in the Albright-Knox Art Gallery, was its assistant treasurer and then was elected to the board of its governing organization, the Buffalo Fine Arts Academy, where his father was a longtime member and president.  
    As attorney for Kissing Bridge Ski Resort, he entered the successful bid to buy the rival Glenwood ski area in the 1970s. He later was Kissing Bridge board chairman.He also served on the boards of several other companies, including Mentholatum, Niagara Blower and Metal Cladding.   He was a past president of the Erie County Mental Health Association, and chaired its 1969 protest on the grounds of the West Seneca State School over the state's failure to open the children's psychiatric hospital that it had built there. He later chaired an Erie County task force on mental health.  
    He served as president of the International Institute of Buffalo and headed its endowment fund drive. He also was a vice president of the Buffalo Council on World Affairs.   He served on many other boards and commissions, including Planned Parenthood, Upstate New York Transplant Services (now ConnectLife), the Buffalo Arts Commission and the Erie County Cultural Resources Advisory Board.   An avid tennis player, he competed in and sometimes organized a long-running tournament between summer residents of Derby and Clarksburg. He later was president of the Buffalo Tennis and Squash Club.  
    He also was an accomplished skier and enjoyed running, and canoe and sailing trips. He renovated classic automobiles, beginning with a 1929 Ford Model A, which he bought for $25 when he was 14. Some of them are on display in the Buffalo Transportation Pierce-Arrow Museum.  
    After his first marriage ended in divorce, he was twice remarried, and was a caregiver to his two wives during the illnesses before their deaths.   In 1974, he became the husband of Louise Lenore Morris. A teacher at Buffalo Seminary and Nichols School, she died in 2006. Louise Terrace at the Burchfield Penney Art Center is dedicated in her honor.   His third wife, the former Linda Robertson, who helped fund the construction of the Magavern-Sutton Courtyard at Buffalo Seminary, died in 2018.  
    Survivors include his daughters, Mary Magavern, Lydia Shrestha and Polly Wolfe; three sisters, Margaret Hargraves, Mary Worrell and Jane Beebe; two stepchildren, Laird Robertson and Megan Robertson; seven grandchildren and four step-grandchildren. His brother James died in 2022.  
    A memorial service will be held at 11 a.m. July 11 in Westminster Presbyterian Church, 724 Delaware Ave.

# BARÇA ACADEMY

The **Barça Academy** is a sports school aimed at boys and girls from 6 to 18 years old which follows and replicates the game model established in the coaching teams at FC Barcelona.

This football school model, exported internationally, aims to extend the Barça brand and transmit the Club's work philosophy and values ​​to the rest of the world.

**Barça Academies** work with their own unique model, based on the Barça methodology used in lower categories to the first team alike , with a proactive, collective and creative style of play, and with an indispensable transmission of values: **respect, humility, effort, ambition and teamwork.**

[Find your Barça Academy](https://barcaacademy.fcbarcelona.com/en/about-us/map)

# BARÇA ACADEMY

The **Barça Academy** is a sports school aimed at boys and girls from 6 to 18 years old which follows and replicates the game model established in the coaching teams at FC Barcelona.

This football school model, exported internationally, aims to extend the Barça brand and transmit the Club's work philosophy and values ​​to the rest of the world.

**Barça Academies** work with their own unique model, based on the Barça methodology used in lower categories to the first team alike , with a proactive, collective and creative style of play, and with an indispensable transmission of values: **respect, humility, effort, ambition and teamwork.**

Barça Academy is a football program that follows the FC Barcelona model aimed at boys and girls from the ages of 5 to 16. We employ the same training methods that are used by the youth teams at the Club.

## Why Plus Codes?

![Image 32](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/9dc3448960e80f72dbccdeed77dcddc8c6fa4da5.svg)

Open source and easy to use

Plus Codes technology is open source and free to create and use. They are much shorter than traditional global coordinates, so they're easy to share.

![Image 33](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/617f07c2232fbfffea814375caf6ff98d9a2b5c9.svg)

Accessible offline

Plus Codes work whether you're online or offline—you don't need an internet connection.

![Image 34](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/0dd4c50ecce352ab4a741db8a640d760806c96ae.svg)

Language independent

Plus Codes are based on a set of 20 alphanumeric characters. They exclude vowels and confusing characters, and are not case-sensitive.

![Image 35](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/651b5eddda4d5b55b913b535752de3cbd9c70488.svg)

Versatile

Plus Codes represent an area. The resolution of the area can be changed by adding or removing characters after the "+" sign.

## Why Plus Codes?

![Image 32](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/9dc3448960e80f72dbccdeed77dcddc8c6fa4da5.svg)

Open source and easy to use

Plus Codes technology is open source and free to create and use. They are much shorter than traditional global coordinates, so they're easy to share.

![Image 33](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/617f07c2232fbfffea814375caf6ff98d9a2b5c9.svg)

Accessible offline

Plus Codes work whether you're online or offline—you don't need an internet connection.

![Image 34](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/0dd4c50ecce352ab4a741db8a640d760806c96ae.svg)

Language independent

Plus Codes are based on a set of 20 alphanumeric characters. They exclude vowels and confusing characters, and are not case-sensitive.

![Image 35](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-mobius-cdn/pluscodes/uploads/651b5eddda4d5b55b913b535752de3cbd9c70488.svg)

Versatile

Plus Codes represent an area. The resolution of the area can be changed by adding or removing characters after the "+" sign.

Hi Owen,

  

this is something that has in fact been discussed both here and in the GitHub repository. Both the full code (8 digits in front of the + sign) and the short code (4 digits in front of +, followed by a reference location) are valid plus codes, and each project using plus codes can decide whether to use one or the other. Google Maps chose to only display short codes with the major difficulty being that a reference location needs to be turned back into coordinates first, making it hard to copy a short code from there to elsewhere and use it without problems (especially offline).

  

While some Googlers are watching this group, it might be best to give feedback via the Google Maps app directly, and request an optional display of full codes as a feature there.

  

In the meantime,https://plus.codes/map has a grid function that you can enable to show full code prefixes for the whole map. I hope that helps with your understanding of what prefix typically addresses what region.

Hi,

  

This is mostly a feature request for Maps, but am happy to learn of alternatives, existing duplicate requests, or correction if I misunderstand anything.  

  

From my OLC specs reading, so far I’m aware that plus codes break down the Earth’s surface into cells with customizable precision (add/remove least significant digits on the right and possibly padding with 0, ex. CCCC0000+ vs CCCCCCCC+CCCC), optional use of a reference location (remove digits from the left and using a landmark name to select outer cell, ex. CCCC+CC City, Province), and the + formatting character to keep track of the place value, analagous to the decimal point.

  

However, when a plus code is given in Google Maps, the **code always uses the same formatting and there isn’t any widget near the given plus code or in Maps configuration to customize it**.

  

![Image 3: pluscode.png](https://groups.google.com/group/open-location-code/attach/7c1ab088ccde0/pluscode.png?part=0.1&view=1)  

  

In my case, I don’t want to use the 6-digit version with a reference location (ex. GGHH+JJ City, Province) and would much prefer the absolute 10-digit equivalent (ex. CCFFGGHH+JJ) to avoid ambiguity and to be more aware of which larger regions correspond to which leftmost digits (ex. I want to recognize what continent/ocean is likely referenced with a CCFF0000+ prefix).

  

Thanks and greetings,

  

Owen

Hi Owen,

  

this is something that has in fact been discussed both here and in the GitHub repository. Both the full code (8 digits in front of the + sign) and the short code (4 digits in front of +, followed by a reference location) are valid plus codes, and each project using plus codes can decide whether to use one or the other. Google Maps chose to only display short codes with the major difficulty being that a reference location needs to be turned back into coordinates first, making it hard to copy a short code from there to elsewhere and use it without problems (especially offline).

  

While some Googlers are watching this group, it might be best to give feedback via the Google Maps app directly, and request an optional display of full codes as a feature there.

  

In the meantime,https://plus.codes/map has a grid function that you can enable to show full code prefixes for the whole map. I hope that helps with your understanding of what prefix typically addresses what region.

# Find & share a location using Plus Codes

You can use and share Plus Codes to:

*   Get and use a simple digital address.
*   Define a specific location for a conventional address. For example, you can identify different entrances to the same building.
*   Identify a specific location to receive deliveries or access emergency and social services.

Here’s an example of a Plus Code: `JJXX+HR8, Seattle`.

## Find & share a location’s Plus Code

1.   On your iPhone or iPad, open the Google Maps app ![Image 1: Maps](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/yBT9NcPCOum61BXUrmlfBecOpNufMGBDbh3rFQfIQu1Rs23tjRnhNdEou6yHAurnyw=h36).
2.   Find the location where you want to get a Plus Code.
3.   To drop a Pin ![Image 2: Explore](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/kd3rLYEzITTexc8oje0I126qWBNfXfsGwAFcCrovyMJpHnj4kzBqZ0YbKajZRc_RE5Y=w36-h36) at the location, tap the screen. 
    *   At the bottom, a panel appears.

4.   To copy the location’s code, in the panel, tap the Plus Code ![Image 3](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/dCChMsdvVBVhqagNl1JkWMYe6JeZmJZViVzBsxntBD6RoXMav923KA3jlH17mKs8Aw9T=w36).
5.   To share the location, paste the Plus Code into the messaging platform of your choice.

## Find & share your current location’s Plus Code

1.   On your iPhone or iPad,open the Google Maps app ![Image 4: Maps](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/yBT9NcPCOum61BXUrmlfBecOpNufMGBDbh3rFQfIQu1Rs23tjRnhNdEou6yHAurnyw=h36).
2.   Tap the blue dot that shows your location. 
    *   At the bottom, the “Your Location” panel appears.

3.   From the bottom of your screen, swipe up until you find the “Plus Code” section.
4.   Tap **Copy code**.
5.   To share the location, paste the Plus Code into the messaging platform of your choice.

If you’re offline, you might find a global Plus Code without a town or city name. Instead, an area code is added to the beginning of the Plus Code, like `9C5M8QQ7+V8`.

## Find a location with a Plus Code

To search for a location with a Plus Code:

1.   On your iPhone or iPad, open the Google Maps app ![Image 5: Maps](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/yBT9NcPCOum61BXUrmlfBecOpNufMGBDbh3rFQfIQu1Rs23tjRnhNdEou6yHAurnyw=h36).
2.   At the top, in the search box, enter the Plus Code. 
    1.   **To search a town or city you’re not currently in:** Enter a Plus Code with a town or city name. For example: `JJXX+HR8, Seattle`.
    2.   **To search a town or city you’re currently in:**Enter only the 6- or 7-digit Plus Code. For example, if you’re in Seattle, you can directly search for `JJXX+HR8`.

[Learn more about Plus Codes](https://plus.codes/).

# Find & share a location using Plus Codes

You can use and share Plus Codes to:

*   Get and use a simple digital address.
*   Define a specific location for a conventional address. For example, you can identify different entrances to the same building.
*   Identify a specific location to receive deliveries or access emergency and social services.

Here’s an example of a Plus Code: `JJXX+HR8, Seattle`.

[iPhone & iPad](https://support.google.com/maps/answer/7047426?hl=en&co=GENIE.Platform=iOS)[Android](https://support.google.com/maps/answer/7047426?hl=en&co=GENIE.Platform=iOS)[Computer](https://support.google.com/maps/answer/7047426?hl=en&co=GENIE.Platform=iOS)

## Find & share a location’s Plus Code

1.   On your iPhone or iPad, open the Google Maps app ![Image 1: Maps](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/yBT9NcPCOum61BXUrmlfBecOpNufMGBDbh3rFQfIQu1Rs23tjRnhNdEou6yHAurnyw=h36).
2.   Find the location where you want to get a Plus Code.
3.   To drop a Pin ![Image 2: Explore](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/kd3rLYEzITTexc8oje0I126qWBNfXfsGwAFcCrovyMJpHnj4kzBqZ0YbKajZRc_RE5Y=w36-h36) at the location, tap the screen. 
    *   At the bottom, a panel appears.

4.   To copy the location’s code, in the panel, tap the Plus Code ![Image 3](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/dCChMsdvVBVhqagNl1JkWMYe6JeZmJZViVzBsxntBD6RoXMav923KA3jlH17mKs8Aw9T=w36).
5.   To share the location, paste the Plus Code into the messaging platform of your choice.

## Find & share your current location’s Plus Code

1.   On your iPhone or iPad,open the Google Maps app ![Image 4: Maps](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/yBT9NcPCOum61BXUrmlfBecOpNufMGBDbh3rFQfIQu1Rs23tjRnhNdEou6yHAurnyw=h36).
2.   Tap the blue dot that shows your location. 
    *   At the bottom, the “Your Location” panel appears.

3.   From the bottom of your screen, swipe up until you find the “Plus Code” section.
4.   Tap **Copy code**.
5.   To share the location, paste the Plus Code into the messaging platform of your choice.

If you’re offline, you might find a global Plus Code without a town or city name. Instead, an area code is added to the beginning of the Plus Code, like `9C5M8QQ7+V8`.

## Find a location with a Plus Code

To search for a location with a Plus Code:

1.   On your iPhone or iPad, open the Google Maps app ![Image 5: Maps](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/yBT9NcPCOum61BXUrmlfBecOpNufMGBDbh3rFQfIQu1Rs23tjRnhNdEou6yHAurnyw=h36).
2.   At the top, in the search box, enter the Plus Code. 
    1.   **To search a town or city you’re not currently in:** Enter a Plus Code with a town or city name. For example: `JJXX+HR8, Seattle`.
    2.   **To search a town or city you’re currently in:**Enter only the 6- or 7-digit Plus Code. For example, if you’re in Seattle, you can directly search for `JJXX+HR8`.

[Learn more about Plus Codes](https://plus.codes/).

For many of us, it’s easy to take addresses for granted. We order products online, and they show up at our doorstep. In an emergency, we give our address to an ambulance or fire truck, and they quickly get to us. But what happens when you don’t have an address and you need to direct someone to your current location?

More than 2 billion people on the planet—about 25 percent of us or more —either don’t have an address or have an address that isn’t easy to locate. To tackle this challenge, we launched [Plus Codes](https://plus.codes/) in 2015. Plus Codes are simple, easy to use digital addresses derived from latitude and longitude coordinates. They can be used to uniquely identify any location, from a rural home out on a prairie to a small shop stall on a nameless street.

Today we’ve made it easier for anyone with an Android device to share their location using Plus Codes in Google Maps. People who use Google Maps might be familiar with the blue dot that represents their current location. Simply tap the blue dot to get a Plus Code for your current location that can be shared with others as easily as giving them a phone number.

![Image 2: Tap the blue dot to get a Plus Code](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/original_images/Plus_Codes_blue_dot.gif)

### Plus Codes: free, digital address for anywhere

A Plus Code is a simple alphanumeric code which can be combined with a locality (for example: FWM8+V9, Ibadan, Nigeria). They look like a regular address, but with a short code where a street name or number would be. Beyond using the blue dot, you can also find the Plus Code for a location by tapping and holding the map to drop a pin at a location you want a Plus Code for.

Plus Codes are searchable on Google Maps and even Google Search, meaning everywhere on the planet can now be uniquely identified.

These digital location identifiers are free to use, available offline and can be printed on paper, posters and signs. The technology to generate Plus Codes is also [open source](https://opensource.google/projects/open-location-code), which means the technology is easy and free to use, so anyone can see how the technology works and develop their own applications for any use case.

![Image 3: About Plus Codes](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/original_images/About_Plus_Codes.gif)

### A helpful tool for emergency and crisis situations

Plus Codes can be especially helpful for people and organizations in emergency and crisis response scenarios. If you’ve ever been in an emergency, you know that being able to share your location for help to easily find you is critical. Yet in many places in the world, organizations struggle with this challenge on a daily basis.

With Plus Codes, not only can people share their location quickly even without an address, but they can now do so by simply opening up Google Maps and tapping on the blue dot to view, copy and share their Plus Code location. A Plus Code can then be entered into Google Maps to help locate and navigate to that location.

Digital locations through Plus Codes means that everywhere now has an easily identifiable location, saving time and getting resources there when it really matters. Not having an address should no longer be a barrier to easily sharing your location with service providers, guiding them to you when you most need them.

Download the latest version of the Google Maps Android app over the coming weeks to try out the new update.

For many of us, it’s easy to take addresses for granted. We order products online, and they show up at our doorstep. In an emergency, we give our address to an ambulance or fire truck, and they quickly get to us. But what happens when you don’t have an address and you need to direct someone to your current location?

More than 2 billion people on the planet—about 25 percent of us or more —either don’t have an address or have an address that isn’t easy to locate. To tackle this challenge, we launched [Plus Codes](https://plus.codes/) in 2015. Plus Codes are simple, easy to use digital addresses derived from latitude and longitude coordinates. They can be used to uniquely identify any location, from a rural home out on a prairie to a small shop stall on a nameless street.

Today we’ve made it easier for anyone with an Android device to share their location using Plus Codes in Google Maps. People who use Google Maps might be familiar with the blue dot that represents their current location. Simply tap the blue dot to get a Plus Code for your current location that can be shared with others as easily as giving them a phone number.

![Image 2: Tap the blue dot to get a Plus Code](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/original_images/Plus_Codes_blue_dot.gif)

### Plus Codes: free, digital address for anywhere

A Plus Code is a simple alphanumeric code which can be combined with a locality (for example: FWM8+V9, Ibadan, Nigeria). They look like a regular address, but with a short code where a street name or number would be. Beyond using the blue dot, you can also find the Plus Code for a location by tapping and holding the map to drop a pin at a location you want a Plus Code for.

Plus Codes are searchable on Google Maps and even Google Search, meaning everywhere on the planet can now be uniquely identified.

These digital location identifiers are free to use, available offline and can be printed on paper, posters and signs. The technology to generate Plus Codes is also [open source](https://opensource.google/projects/open-location-code), which means the technology is easy and free to use, so anyone can see how the technology works and develop their own applications for any use case.

![Image 3: About Plus Codes](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/original_images/About_Plus_Codes.gif)

### A helpful tool for emergency and crisis situations

Plus Codes can be especially helpful for people and organizations in emergency and crisis response scenarios. If you’ve ever been in an emergency, you know that being able to share your location for help to easily find you is critical. Yet in many places in the world, organizations struggle with this challenge on a daily basis.

With Plus Codes, not only can people share their location quickly even without an address, but they can now do so by simply opening up Google Maps and tapping on the blue dot to view, copy and share their Plus Code location. A Plus Code can then be entered into Google Maps to help locate and navigate to that location.

Digital locations through Plus Codes means that everywhere now has an easily identifiable location, saving time and getting resources there when it really matters. Not having an address should no longer be a barrier to easily sharing your location with service providers, guiding them to you when you most need them.

Download the latest version of the Google Maps Android app over the coming weeks to try out the new update.

Overview

Plus codes make location information easier to use. Instead of two long numbers (atitude and longitude) there's a single, shorter code.

Most people in the world live on an unnamed street. Plus codes were created so that these people can have an address, so that they can receive deliveries, access emergency services, register to vote – and more. Plus codes are open source and free to use, for any purpose, forever.

Plus codes are based on latitude and longitude, so they already exist everywhere. The location 47°21'56.0"N 8°31'29.3"E has the plus code "8FVC9G8F+6W".

Plus codes can be converted to plus code addresses. These use place names and a short version of the code: "9G8F+6W, Zürich, Switzerland". This form is easier to recognise, and the shorter code means people have less digits to remember.

This add-on for Google Sheets allows you to convert between location coordinates and plus codes, using a menu function and additional sheet functions:

*  PLUSCODE
*  PLUSCODE_CENTER
*  PLUSCODE_LENGTH
*  PLUSCODE_BOUNDS

You can also convert between plus codes and addresses using the menu and additional functions:

*  PLUSCODE_TO_ADDRESS
*  PLUSCODE_FROM_ADDRESS

Plus codes use the Open Location Code algorithm, an open source Google project. See https://opensource.google.com/projects/open-location-code for links to the open source projects.

Overview

Plus codes make location information easier to use. Instead of two long numbers (atitude and longitude) there's a single, shorter code.

Most people in the world live on an unnamed street. Plus codes were created so that these people can have an address, so that they can receive deliveries, access emergency services, register to vote – and more. Plus codes are open source and free to use, for any purpose, forever.

Plus codes are based on latitude and longitude, so they already exist everywhere. The location 47°21'56.0"N 8°31'29.3"E has the plus code "8FVC9G8F+6W".

Plus codes can be converted to plus code addresses. These use place names and a short version of the code: "9G8F+6W, Zürich, Switzerland". This form is easier to recognise, and the shorter code means people have less digits to remember.

This add-on for Google Sheets allows you to convert between location coordinates and plus codes, using a menu function and additional sheet functions:

*  PLUSCODE
*  PLUSCODE_CENTER
*  PLUSCODE_LENGTH
*  PLUSCODE_BOUNDS

You can also convert between plus codes and addresses using the menu and additional functions:

*  PLUSCODE_TO_ADDRESS
*  PLUSCODE_FROM_ADDRESS

Plus codes use the Open Location Code algorithm, an open source Google project. See https://opensource.google.com/projects/open-location-code for links to the open source projects.

# What Are Google Maps Plus Codes? And Some Great Free Alternatives

by Placekey

Google Maps Plus Codes is a location identification system like [Placekey](https://www.google.ca/maps) that works with [Google Maps](https://www.google.ca/maps) to allow you to easily create, use, and share address data.

While this solution is extremely easy to use, there are a number reasons why Google Maps Plus Codes is not the best current location mapping and tracking solution. To help you understand why and point you in the right direction (pun intended!), we’ll cover the following:

*   What are Google Plus Codes & location keys?
*   How do Google Maps Plus Codes work?
*   How to find and share locations with a Plus Code
*   Why location keys are better than Google Plus Codes  

To start, let’s cover the difference between location keys and Google Maps Plus Codes.

## What are Google Plus Codes & location keys?

[Google Plus Map Codes](https://maps.google.com/pluscodes/technology/) are location keys that represent street addresses as alphanumeric codes based on latitude and longitude. They are open-source, free, and easy to access and use. They can be used to receive deliveries, access emergency and social services, and otherwise help people map or find an address.

![Image 3: How Google Maps Plus Codes work](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/68f27fcf379331a1a5acc995/68f27fcf379331a1a5acd301_60733fbf22bccabdf2b7400b_how-google-maps-plus-codes-work.jpeg)

_Image Credit_: [Google Plus Codes Technology](https://maps.google.com/pluscodes/technology/)

Plus Codes are a form of location key, which is essentially any alphanumeric code that represents a physical location. These are commonly used for street addresses, but can be used to identify and label any real-world location.

This is better than traditional addressing, as you can create a Plus Code for any location, even if it does not have a standardized (or even existing) street address. This is ideally suited for people that live in rural areas and don’t have access to an address. Plus Codes provide an alternative for those that do not have a street address, giving them access to an address for mailing, emergency services, and more. When we get into rural areas, where most locations have street addresses, Placekey is a more accurate, powerful solution, as you can encode multiple POIs to a single location!

Plus Codes uses open-source technology, and is therefore free to create and use by anyone. Their simplified, shortened, and standardized format make them extremely easy to work with and share with others.

## How do Google Maps Plus Codes work?

Plus Codes are alphanumeric codes that represent latitude and longitude coordinates. This code is based on a division of the globe using a **square grid system** based on latitude/longitude WGS84. The final portion of the Plus Code reflects a unique address within this grid, and the preceding portion of the code identifies the cell this location is in.

Google Maps Plus Codes work by converting location coordinates (latitude and longitude) to alphanumeric codes that use a standardized format. They use an alphanumeric grid (like a chess board with a grid of A - H and 1 - 8) to divide the world.

![Image 4: How the Google Maps Plus Code grid system works](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/68f27fcf379331a1a5acc995/68f27fcf379331a1a5acd305_60733fdb35c4a2271f79a4c1_google-maps-grid-system.jpeg)

_Image Credit_: [Google Plus Codes Technology](https://maps.google.com/pluscodes/technology/)

That first grid forms the first 2 numbers of the code. That square is then further subdivided, forming the next portion of the Plus Code. The result is an extremely easy-to-use code that represents a unique address in the world.

Whether you create the Plus Codes yourself or you are using Plus Codes that others have created, you can then use these Plus Codes to manage addresses. These codes are less prone to spelling and formatting errors, making them easier to work with.

Developers can easily use Plus Codes to build flexible, personalized, and easily shareable address solutions from the open-source technology available.

Google Plus Codes can also easily be used with the Google Maps platform, enabling you to pair this data with the Places API and Geocoding API so that you can enter and retrieve this information as needed. There are also a number of add-ons available for Plus Codes that enhance what you can use them for, such as the Google Sheets Add-on or the Grid Service Add-on.

[![Image 5: Why Placekeys are better than Plus Codes](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/68f27fcf379331a1a5acc995/68f27fcf379331a1a5acd307_60733ff8e5f2ce85b7ebcb3c_plus-codes-vs-placekeys.png)](https://www.placekey.io/blog/plus-codes-vs-placekeys)
‍

## How to find and share locations with a Plus Code

The main benefit of Plus Code is the simplicity and ease of use. You can quickly and easily find a Plus Code using Google Maps, and then share this with others. All you need to do is:

*   Open Google Maps via an app or mobile web browser
*   Select the location on the map that you need a Plus Code for
*   Copy the Plus Code
*   Send the Plus Code to the person you want to share it with

2.   Using the map, find the location that you want to get a Plus Code for. Touch and hold the screen to place a **Pin**on the map, marking the location you want to get a Plus Code for.
3.   Along the bottom, tap “Dropped pin”.
4.   Beside the **Plus Code logo**, find the Plus Code. (i.e. 8QQ7+V8, Dublin).
5.   Tap the **Plus Code** to copy a location’s code.
6.   You can then paste the Plus Code in another messaging service (email, direct messaging service, etc.) to share the location.

### How to find and share a location’s Plus Code using an iPhone or iPad

2.   Using the map, find the location that you want to get a Plus Code for. Touch and hold the screen to place a **Pin**on the map, marking the location you want to get a Plus Code for.

4.   Beside the **Plus Code logo**, find the Plus Code. (i.e. 8QQ7+V8, Dublin).
5.   Tap the **Plus Code** to copy a location’s code.
6.   You can then paste the Plus Code in another messaging service (email, direct messaging service, etc.) to share the location.

6.   You can then paste the Plus Code in another messaging service (email, direct messaging service, etc.) to share the location.

Open Location Code is an open-source technology that allows you to encode location information (latitude and longitude) in an easier to use format. These codes allow you to create a location code for addresses that are otherwise unable to be mapped, such as those without street addresses.

One main advantage of using a software library is that this can be done offline, as the program is performing the task for you, without needing to connect to another solution or integration.

## Why location keys are better than Google Plus Codes

Google Plus Codes and location keys are both standardized location identifiers that simplify address management. However, location keys like [Placekey](https://www.placekey.io/) have greater capabilities, the most important of which is that they allow you to track points of interest at specific addresses. With this, you can not only identify **where**things are, but you can also map **what**things are at those locations.

![Image 6: The breakdown of a Placekey’s what and where](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/68f27fcf379331a1a5acc995/68f27fcf379331a1a5acd2fe_66e1e0fb2c44a18683fc2df4_602a731071f397b2bd561215_placekey.png)

Placekey uses this **what**at the **where**system to track points of interest (POIs) at different addresses, represented by easy-to-use alphanumeric codes. While Google Plus Codes use a grid to encode location and address data, Placekey has an added layer that encodes a POI.

While Plus Codes allow you to create unique location keys for specific locations, Placekey goes a step further, allowing you to identify multiple POIs at a single address or location. This empowers users to identify and track multiple places at a single address, or even the changing places of an address over time. This can be ideal for tracking the different stores at a mall (which is one single address) or multiple business offices in a skyscraper.

This can be used to map, manage, and share locations with ease. As a free, universal solution, the Placekey community is able to develop their own unique solutions, all leveraging the [Placekey universal identification system](https://h3geo.org/).

Plus Code uses a traditional grid system to divide the globe. This square system is inferior to the hexagonal grid system that Placekey uses, which is the [H3](https://h3geo.org/) Hexagonal hierarchical spatial index system also [used by Uber](https://eng.uber.com/h3/).

While squares are good for dividing a flat object, hexagons are better for dividing a spherical object with accuracy. As opposed to a square, all outside points are equidistant to the centre of a hexagon, providing a more accurate method of mapping. This means that you can draw more meaningful insights from this data and apply them quicker and with confidence.

Plus Codes are intended to help identify locations and typically represent a 14 meter x 14 meter space (roughly the size of half of a basketball court), but can work at multiple resolutions. They were not built to convey POI-related information whatsoever, nor can they distinguish between places on different floors within a building (i.e. specific apartment units) or individual, smaller POIs within a larger footprint (i.e. Starbucks coffee shop within a Target retail store).

In short, a Placekey can provide all of the information available in a Plus Code, but then takes it a big step further by providing an extra layer of POI-related information for added precision that can unlock a wealth of unique insights when joined with multiple datasets.

# What Are Google Maps Plus Codes? And Some Great Free Alternatives

by Placekey

Google Maps Plus Codes is a location identification system like [Placekey](https://www.google.ca/maps) that works with [Google Maps](https://www.google.ca/maps) to allow you to easily create, use, and share address data.

While this solution is extremely easy to use, there are a number reasons why Google Maps Plus Codes is not the best current location mapping and tracking solution. To help you understand why and point you in the right direction (pun intended!), we’ll cover the following:

*   What are Google Plus Codes & location keys?
*   How do Google Maps Plus Codes work?
*   How to find and share locations with a Plus Code
*   Why location keys are better than Google Plus Codes  

To start, let’s cover the difference between location keys and Google Maps Plus Codes.

## What are Google Plus Codes & location keys?

[Google Plus Map Codes](https://maps.google.com/pluscodes/technology/) are location keys that represent street addresses as alphanumeric codes based on latitude and longitude. They are open-source, free, and easy to access and use. They can be used to receive deliveries, access emergency and social services, and otherwise help people map or find an address.

![Image 3: How Google Maps Plus Codes work](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/68f27fcf379331a1a5acc995/68f27fcf379331a1a5acd301_60733fbf22bccabdf2b7400b_how-google-maps-plus-codes-work.jpeg)

_Image Credit_: [Google Plus Codes Technology](https://maps.google.com/pluscodes/technology/)

Plus Codes are a form of location key, which is essentially any alphanumeric code that represents a physical location. These are commonly used for street addresses, but can be used to identify and label any real-world location.

This is better than traditional addressing, as you can create a Plus Code for any location, even if it does not have a standardized (or even existing) street address. This is ideally suited for people that live in rural areas and don’t have access to an address. Plus Codes provide an alternative for those that do not have a street address, giving them access to an address for mailing, emergency services, and more. When we get into rural areas, where most locations have street addresses, Placekey is a more accurate, powerful solution, as you can encode multiple POIs to a single location!

Plus Codes uses open-source technology, and is therefore free to create and use by anyone. Their simplified, shortened, and standardized format make them extremely easy to work with and share with others.

## How do Google Maps Plus Codes work?

Plus Codes are alphanumeric codes that represent latitude and longitude coordinates. This code is based on a division of the globe using a **square grid system** based on latitude/longitude WGS84. The final portion of the Plus Code reflects a unique address within this grid, and the preceding portion of the code identifies the cell this location is in.

Google Maps Plus Codes work by converting location coordinates (latitude and longitude) to alphanumeric codes that use a standardized format. They use an alphanumeric grid (like a chess board with a grid of A - H and 1 - 8) to divide the world.

![Image 4: How the Google Maps Plus Code grid system works](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/68f27fcf379331a1a5acc995/68f27fcf379331a1a5acd305_60733fdb35c4a2271f79a4c1_google-maps-grid-system.jpeg)

_Image Credit_: [Google Plus Codes Technology](https://maps.google.com/pluscodes/technology/)

That first grid forms the first 2 numbers of the code. That square is then further subdivided, forming the next portion of the Plus Code. The result is an extremely easy-to-use code that represents a unique address in the world.

Whether you create the Plus Codes yourself or you are using Plus Codes that others have created, you can then use these Plus Codes to manage addresses. These codes are less prone to spelling and formatting errors, making them easier to work with.

Developers can easily use Plus Codes to build flexible, personalized, and easily shareable address solutions from the open-source technology available.

Google Plus Codes can also easily be used with the Google Maps platform, enabling you to pair this data with the Places API and Geocoding API so that you can enter and retrieve this information as needed. There are also a number of add-ons available for Plus Codes that enhance what you can use them for, such as the Google Sheets Add-on or the Grid Service Add-on.

Alternatively, you can use the [Plus Codes Google Sheets Add-on](https://gsuite.google.com/marketplace/app/plus_codes/604254879289?pann=cwsdp&hl=en-GB), which allows you to convert location coordinates to plus codes, and vice versa. This is made possible by menu function and dynamic sheet functions, including:

*   PLUSCODE
*   PLUSCODE_CENTER
*   PLUSCODE_LENGTH
*   PLUSCODE_BOUNDS  

You are also able to convert plus codes and addresses with ease using:

*   PLUSCODE_TO_ADDRESS
*   PLUSCODE_FROM_ADDRESS  

These functions can be used to simplify the process of managing, finding, and sharing plus codes, all within Google Sheets.

### How to find and share a location’s Plus Code using an API or Professional Software

To simplify the process of finding and sharing Plus Codes, you can use an API or a professional software. Unlike using Google Sheets or manually creating your own system, these are designed to perform these functions for you, making it easier to find, share, and manage Plus Codes.

For example, the [Plus Codes Grid Service](https://www.google.com/earth/) lets you integrate the Plus Codes grid to online maps and other GIS applications that you are using. You can do this using a variety of APIs, softwares, and other solutions, including:

*   **Image tiles**: users can display the grid on online maps and GIS applications (such as ArcGIS, QGIS, and arguably the simplest option - Google Maps)
*   **GeoJSON**: leverages vector data to draw the grid on maps using JavaScript libraries, automating much of the process.
*   **Keyhole Markup Language (KML)**: displays the grid within [Google Earth](https://www.google.com/earth/) for ease-of-use.  

Ultimately, these integrations allow you to leverage Google Plus Codes and the grid by integrating them directly with your geocoding and address management solutions.

## Why location keys are better than Google Plus Codes

Google Plus Codes and location keys are both standardized location identifiers that simplify address management. However, location keys like [Placekey](https://www.placekey.io/) have greater capabilities, the most important of which is that they allow you to track points of interest at specific addresses. With this, you can not only identify **where**things are, but you can also map **what**things are at those locations.

![Image 6: The breakdown of a Placekey’s what and where](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/68f27fcf379331a1a5acc995/68f27fcf379331a1a5acd2fe_66e1e0fb2c44a18683fc2df4_602a731071f397b2bd561215_placekey.png)

Placekey uses this **what**at the **where**system to track points of interest (POIs) at different addresses, represented by easy-to-use alphanumeric codes. While Google Plus Codes use a grid to encode location and address data, Placekey has an added layer that encodes a POI.

While Plus Codes allow you to create unique location keys for specific locations, Placekey goes a step further, allowing you to identify multiple POIs at a single address or location. This empowers users to identify and track multiple places at a single address, or even the changing places of an address over time. This can be ideal for tracking the different stores at a mall (which is one single address) or multiple business offices in a skyscraper.

This can be used to map, manage, and share locations with ease. As a free, universal solution, the Placekey community is able to develop their own unique solutions, all leveraging the [Placekey universal identification system](https://h3geo.org/).

Plus Code uses a traditional grid system to divide the globe. This square system is inferior to the hexagonal grid system that Placekey uses, which is the [H3](https://h3geo.org/) Hexagonal hierarchical spatial index system also [used by Uber](https://eng.uber.com/h3/).

While squares are good for dividing a flat object, hexagons are better for dividing a spherical object with accuracy. As opposed to a square, all outside points are equidistant to the centre of a hexagon, providing a more accurate method of mapping. This means that you can draw more meaningful insights from this data and apply them quicker and with confidence.

Plus Codes are intended to help identify locations and typically represent a 14 meter x 14 meter space (roughly the size of half of a basketball court), but can work at multiple resolutions. They were not built to convey POI-related information whatsoever, nor can they distinguish between places on different floors within a building (i.e. specific apartment units) or individual, smaller POIs within a larger footprint (i.e. Starbucks coffee shop within a Target retail store).

In short, a Placekey can provide all of the information available in a Plus Code, but then takes it a big step further by providing an extra layer of POI-related information for added precision that can unlock a wealth of unique insights when joined with multiple datasets.

Here we’ll briefly explain what plus codes are, their intent, and how you can use them on Google Maps.

## What Are Google Maps Plus Codes?

Every spot on Earth can be located [using latitude and longitude coordinates](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/find-longitude-latitude/). However, this long string of numbers isn’t always the most convenient way to find a place. With this in mind, Google’s Zürich engineering office released the [Open Location Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Location_Code), known as the “plus code,” in 2014.

[![Image 3: What Are Google Maps Plus Codes? image - image-52](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-52.png)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-52.png)

A plus code is a shortcode version of traditional location coordinates. With a grid system, the plus code is created by zooming in on that specific location on the grid. Using a combination of sequential labels for rows and columns and alphanumeric characters, you arrive at a plus code like this: 4RXV+29 Las Vegas, Nevada.

The intent of plus codes is to provide every location, no matter how remote, with a recognizable “address.” So those places without street names or exact street addresses can still be located with pinpoint precision for things like deliveries, emergency services, and social services.

[![Image 4: What Are Google Maps Plus Codes? image 2 - image-53](blob:http://localhost/e2c4315f43d718dcb376aec238de6520)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-53.png)

Plus codes are free and work offline. Visit the Google Maps Plus Codes website for complete details, the technology behind them, common questions, and finding your home or current location plus code.

# What Are Google Maps Plus Codes and How to Use Them

Maybe you’ve heard about Google Maps plus codes but haven’t had time to learn more. Or perhaps you’ve seen plus codes for locations when using Google Maps and wondered what they were.

Here we’ll briefly explain what plus codes are, their intent, and how you can use them on Google Maps.

Download Interactive Maps

## What Are Google Maps Plus Codes?

Every spot on Earth can be located [using latitude and longitude coordinates](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/find-longitude-latitude/). However, this long string of numbers isn’t always the most convenient way to find a place. With this in mind, Google’s Zürich engineering office released the [Open Location Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Location_Code), known as the “plus code,” in 2014.

[![Image 3: What Are Google Maps Plus Codes? image - image-52](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-52.png)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-52.png)

A plus code is a shortcode version of traditional location coordinates. With a grid system, the plus code is created by zooming in on that specific location on the grid. Using a combination of sequential labels for rows and columns and alphanumeric characters, you arrive at a plus code like this: 4RXV+29 Las Vegas, Nevada.

Master Coding Skills

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LJ9zEkXearU)

The intent of plus codes is to provide every location, no matter how remote, with a recognizable “address.” So those places without street names or exact street addresses can still be located with pinpoint precision for things like deliveries, emergency services, and social services.

[![Image 4: What Are Google Maps Plus Codes? image 2 - image-53](blob:http://localhost/e2c4315f43d718dcb376aec238de6520)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-53.png)

Plus codes are free and work offline. Visit the Google Maps Plus Codes website for complete details, the technology behind them, common questions, and finding your home or current location plus code.

## Find a Plus Code for a Location on the Web

You can find a plus code for a spot whether you use the map view or [the Search feature](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/how-to-view-your-google-maps-search-history/) on the Google Maps website.

#### Google Maps Map View

1.   Visit [Google Maps](https://www.google.com/maps/) and use the map view to choose a location. 
2.   When the detail box appears at the bottom, select the latitude and longitude coordinates displayed.

[![Image 5: Find a Plus Code for a Location on the Web image - image-54](blob:http://localhost/f724f90f395ce0ac06d0733111c5e71b)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-54.png)

1.   This opens a sidebar on the left with the location details. Below the city and state, you’ll see the plus code to the right of the code logo.

[![Image 6: Find a Plus Code for a Location on the Web image 2 - image-55](blob:http://localhost/a027c76f11d95641ac73f5a938ebf9e6)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-55.png)

Select the plus code or the **copy** icon to copy it to your clipboard.

Try CAD Software

#### Google Maps Search Feature

1.   Visit [Google Maps](https://www.google.com/maps/) and use the Search box to find the location. You may see the plus code in the details for the search results in the sidebar.

[![Image 7: Find a Plus Code for a Location on the Web image 3 - image-56](blob:http://localhost/85251e3db0e2409495e91a044e049b4d)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-56.png)

1.   If you don’t see the plus code there, right-click the spot on the map and select the latitude and longitude coordinates. This copies them to your clipboard.

[![Image 8: Find a Plus Code for a Location on the Web image 4 - image-57](blob:http://localhost/ae8ce4809c45d17dd9ab96f00086be60)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-57.png)

1.   Paste the latitude and longitude into the Search box. You’ll see the plus code in the sidebar below the city and state.

[![Image 9: Find a Plus Code for a Location on the Web image 5 - image-58](blob:http://localhost/2c8b444be66c0f44b647e1d5d256620c)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-58.png)

Select the plus code or the **copy** icon to copy it to your clipboard.

## Find a Plus Code for a Location in the Mobile App

Open the Google Maps app on Android or iPhone. Like on the website, you can obtain the plus code for a location using map view or the Search box.

#### Google Maps Map View

1.   The quickest way to get a specific location’s plus code using map view is to [drop a pin](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/how-to-drop-a-pin-in-google-maps-on-desktop-and-mobile/). On Android, tap and hold. On iPhone, tap. 
2.   After you drop the pin, swipe up from the bottom of the screen to view the details.
3.   You should see the plus code near the latitude and longitude. If necessary, tap **See all** to expand the information.

[![Image 10: Find a Plus Code for a Location in the Mobile App image - image-59](blob:http://localhost/9e02b3eb860587b4c3fa79c229f86ee1)](https://www.online-tech-tips.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/image-59.png)
